news.title: Judge drops case against Nevada electors accused of forging certificate in 2020 election
news.text: LAS VEGAS — The yearslong case against six Nevada Republicans who were accused of submitting a bogus certificate that falsely declared Donald Trump the winner of the state’s 2020 presidential election has been dismissed, a judge ruled Thursday. The dismissal marks the latest setback in swing states’ efforts to prosecute fake electors who tried to keep Trump in the White House after he lost to Joe Biden in 2020. Three other fake elector cases in Arizona, Michigan and Georgia have been dismissed. Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes recently dismissed her office’s criminal case but vowed to bring it back to a grand jury in hopes of securing another indictment. The dismissal was a legal maneuver aimed at getting around a deadline for starting new grand jury proceedings after Mayes lost an appeal earlier in June. Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford, who is also running for governor as a Democrat, brought charges relating to forgery and “offering a false instrument for filing or record” against the six Nevada Republicans, who pleaded not guilty. His office plans to appeal the ruling. The defendants included Michael McDonald, the chair of the Nevada Republican Party, and Jesse Law, the former chair of the Clark County Republican Party. Their attorneys declined to comment Thursday. After the 2020 election, the six Republican electors gathered outside of the Nevada Legislature to sign a certificate giving the state’s six electoral votes to Trump, despite Biden winning the state by more than 30,000 votes. The ceremony was broadcast online, and the video footage was used as evidence in the case. The case has revolved around the defendants’ intent behind submitting the certificate. Prosecutors argue the defendants intended for their documents to be mistaken for actual electoral votes that then-Vice President Mike Pence would count on Jan. 6, 2021. The defendants say submitting the certificate was an act of “political theater” designed to publicize their concerns about the election. They were preserving their rights to challenge the official election results and had no intent to deceive a government agency into accepting the GOP certificate as real, their attorneys argued. Nevada Judge Mary Kay Holthus agreed. She found there was a lack of evidence that showed the electors intended to deceive government officials, and she determined that the state failed to disclose exculpatory evidence to the grand jury. “The fact that Defendants openly announced both their actions and their asserted purpose, rather than concealing their conduct or attempting to secretly induce governmental reliance, weighs against a reasonable inference that they acted with fraudulent intent,” Holthus wrote in her ruling. Jurisdiction had also been an issue, but the case eventually landed in Clark County, which is home to Las Vegas and leans Democratic. Courts have dismissed similar cases in Michigan and Georgia, and a special prosecutor dropped a federal case in late 2024 that charged Trump with conspiring to overturn the 2020 election. Those cases ended after Trump defeated Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. A fake electors case is ongoing in Wisconsin.

news.title: Fox News Poll: A Senate battle looms in Michigan
news.text: In Michigan, while more Democrats than Republicans are concerned about their candidates’ ideological views, Democrats are also more engaged and enthusiastic about the upcoming election, setting up a battle in the Wolverine State. After a heated Democratic primary, progressive Abdul El-Sayed secured the Senate nomination and will face Republican Mike Rogers this fall as Democrats try to retake the Senate. According to a Fox News survey of Michigan registered voters, Rogers has the edge in the race with 51% to El-Sayed’s 47%, within the survey’s margin of sampling error. FOX NEWS POLL: NEW MATCHUP, SAME RESULT: MAINE SENATE RACE STAYS LOCKED Rogers’ edge comes mostly from greater party unity among Republicans. Nearly all Republicans (96%), including both MAGA (99%) and non-MAGA Republicans (89%), back Rogers. Only a week after winning the primary race, 9 in 10 Democrats (91%) and nearly all Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) supporters (98%) back El-Sayed, but that falls to 69% among non-DSA Democrats and independents. The small subgroup of independents narrowly favors Rogers. El-Sayed’s coalition includes liberal voters, Black voters, urban residents and women with a college degree. Rogers’ most loyal groups are conservatives, White evangelical Christians, rural voters and White men without a degree. Men favor Rogers by 11 points (44% El-Sayed vs. 55% Rogers), while women are split (49-48%). President Donald Trump won the Wolverine State in 2016 and 2024, each time by less than 2 points, while former President Joe Biden won by nearly 3 points in 2020. El-Sayed is underperforming with Black voters, women and suburban voters compared with former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. Rogers similarly trails Trump’s 2024 support among voters under age 30 and independents. That’s according to the 2024 Michigan Fox News Voter Analysis (FNVA). Voter enthusiasm for their candidate is evident on both sides. About three-quarters of each candidate’s supporters are certain they will stick with their choice this fall, and about two-thirds say their support is mainly for their candidate rather than against his opponent. FOX NEWS POLL: GOP DIVISIONS SHAPE TEXAS SENATE RACE El-Sayed leads among the most engaged voters with an 11-point advantage among those extremely interested in the election, a 7-point lead among those extremely motivated and a 4-point edge among definite voters (10-out-of-10 likelihood). Moreover, more Democrats than Republicans are extremely interested (+15 points), motivated to vote (+11) and certain they will cast a ballot this November (+7). More than half the electorate is concerned El-Sayed’s positions on the issues are too extreme (54%) and that Rogers is too close to Trump (51%). Voters on both sides of the aisle share concerns about their candidate’s ideological positioning. Twice as many Democrats are concerned El-Sayed is too extreme (30%) as Republicans are that Rogers is too close to Trump (14%). By a 10-point margin, more independents are concerned about Rogers’ ties to Trump than El-Sayed’s issue positions (58% vs. 48%). Trump’s favorable rating is underwater by 19 points in Michigan (40% favorable, 59% unfavorable). Both Senate candidates also have negative ratings, with El-Sayed (-13 points) faring worse than Rogers (-6). The two major political parties are viewed negatively. The Republican Party has a -12 net favorable rating while the Democratic Party is at -13. "The energy is on the left in Michigan, as it is throughout the country, and that should help with turnout," said Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who helps conduct Fox News polls with Democrat Chris Anderson. "But El-Sayed’s nomination path highlighted party rifts. He needs to reassure a wide range of Michigan Democrats — including Reagan Democrats, Jewish voters and Black voters — that he will serve their interests rather than pursue an extremist agenda." The MAGA movement is viewed more favorably than the DSA by 10 points (40% vs. 30%). However, more voters have strongly unfavorable views of MAGA than DSA (45% vs. 37%). Inflation is the top issue in the Michigan Senate race at 38%, and economic anxiety remains palpable, with 4 in 10 saying they are falling behind financially. Other voter priorities are immigration/border security and healthcare (14% each) and political divisions (11%). El-Sayed stays competitive thanks to voters who prioritize inflation (+10 points), healthcare (+47) and political divisions (+5), while most immigration voters prefer Rogers (+82). Those who say they are falling behind financially also back El-Sayed by 24 points. By an 11-point margin, Michiganders oppose the U.S. continuing to provide military aid to the Israeli government (44% favor vs. 55% oppose). Those favoring aid back Rogers by 45 points, while those opposed prefer El-Sayed by 29 points. Turning to the governor’s race … With Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer term-limited, Michigan’s gubernatorial seat is up for grabs. The Fox News poll finds Democrat Jocelyn Benson has the advantage over Republican John James by 5 points in the governor’s contest (52% vs. 47%). The results fall within the survey’s margin of sampling error. Compared with El-Sayed, Benson draws greater support among non-DSA Democrats and independents: 81% favor Benson in the governor’s race vs. 69% for El-Sayed in the Senate race. There is some ticket-splitting with Rogers’ backers nearly three times as likely to cross over for Benson as El-Sayed supporters are to back James (14% vs. 5%). Benson’s net personal favorable rating is +7 (49% favorable, 42% unfavorable), while James is at -3 (41% favorable, 44% unfavorable). Conducted Aug. 6-10, 2026, under the joint direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News Poll includes interviews with a sample of 1,006 Michigan registered voters randomly selected from a statewide voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (103) and cellphones (654) or completed the survey online after receiving a text message (249). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ±3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis and voter file data. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education and area variables to ensure the demographics of respondents are representative of the registered voter population. Results among subgroups are only shown when the sample size is at least N=100.

news.title: DNC closes ranks around Ken Martin as party weighs official stance on Israel and ICE
news.text:
Martin also faced heavy criticism for the handling of an incomplete 2024 election autopsy that answered few questions about former Vice President Kamala Harris’s loss to President Donald Trump.

Two months after the shelved autopsy report was released, revelations that Martin threw a phone at the desk of a junior staffer, asked vendors not to bill the DNC until after the midterm elections, and used DNC headquarters as collateral for a $15 million line of credit reignited calls from Democrats outside the committee for Martin to resign.

But at the DNC’s Resolutions Committee meeting Thursday, members publicly praised Martin’s leadership and pushed back against the Democratic infighting that has spilled into public view.

“Are you tired of hearing everyone criticize us for not working?” Bill Owen, a Tennessee DNC member, asked. “I think all of us are working as hard as we can to elect Democrats, and this goes … especially to our friends at Morning Joe and Joe Scarborough. I’m tired of him ragging on our chair, Ken Martin. Ken Martin’s a passionate guy.”

Democrats have overperformed in the majority of state and federal elections since Trump began his second term. In April, Democrats expanded their majority on Wisconsin’s Supreme Court. The next month, they held on to control of the Michigan state Senate.

Yet the party remains deeply divided over how to rebuild after its 2024 losses. An insurgent socialist wing, led by New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, has toppled several incumbent Democrats this midterm cycle. Tensions over U.S. support for Israel continue to dominate the primaries.

DNC FACES QUESTIONS OF RELEVANCY IN WAKE OF KEN MARTIN’S SCANDALS

In Michigan, progressive Abdul el Sayed defeated Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI) for the Democratic Senate nomination after regularly criticizing Israel and accusing it of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee spent millions of dollars unsuccessfully opposing el Sayed’s bid against the pro-Israel Stevens.

Those divisions have also spilled into the DNC itself.

Ron Harris, cochair of the DNC resolutions committee, provided members with an update on the Middle East Working Group’s plans. The group was created by Martin last year to hammer out the party’s official stance on Israel and Gaza.

“The group continues to meet and has sketched out a plan to hold a series of sessions with affinity groups, with pollsters, policy experts, and others,” Harris said. “And members will have the opportunities to both listen to these sessions and contribute questions.”

The party’s divisions were even more apparent Thursday during a lengthy debate over a resolution calling for the formal abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Some members sought to amend the resolution to call for reforming ICE rather than abolishing it.

“We’ve adopted resolutions to reform ICE in the past, including the spring meeting in New Orleans, we’ve also just adopted a strong resolution from Chair Martin on the same topic,” said Marge Hoffa, a Minnesota DNC member. “We shouldn’t contradict ourselves by also introducing a resolution that would now call to abolish something that we have a well-established track record of calling to be drastically reformed.”

Members at its 2025 summer meeting denounced the Trump administration’s deportation tactics but stopped short of the calls to “abolish ICE.”

At an April meeting this year, the DNC approved a resolution calling for the replacement of the current structure of ICE to rein in the “lawless conduct of federal immigration enforcement agents.” Another resolution, “demanding improvements and accountability in ICE Detention Facilities, and opposing abusive facilities” was also passed.

On Thursday, the DNC’s resolution committee approved the abolish ICE initiative in a 25-12 vote with one abstention. It now heads to the full DNC for a vote, which is expected either Friday or Saturday.

“Democrats are the open borders party,” Natalie Baldassarre, the RNC’s national press secretary, said shortly after the resolution advanced. “Their radical pro-criminal agenda puts law enforcement and the public at risk. President Trump secured our border, deported violent criminal aliens, and delivered the lowest murder rate in 125 years. If Democrats had any backbone they’d vote down this dangerous proposal and put American citizens first.”

DNC members noted that the resolution is not legally binding but more of a symbolic tool for the Democratic base.

“At the end of the day, this is a resolution passed by the Democratic National Committee,” said Harini Krishnan, a California DNC member. “It does not have any legal binding on the DHS, but what it does do is send a message to voters who have moved left on this issue; it doesn’t matter what state you live in in this country. Voters are asking for us to hold ICE accountable and ICE out. … This resolution is exactly what we need to send a message that, as a Democratic National Committee, we do not stand for this.”

The DNC declined to comment when asked by the Washington Examiner.

DNC PANEL ADVANCES SOUTH CAROLINA AS FIRST STATE IN THE 2028 PRIMARY CALENDAR

John McCarthy, a New Jersey DNC member, defended the debate to the Washington Examiner, saying that “public support for ICE drop kind of across the board.”

“This is something where I think that voters certainly said immigration was an issue that they cared about,” he said. “What the Trump administration has done, especially in some of these cities where they have just been agitators, you know, people didn’t vote for that either.”

news.title: Drama breaks out at DNC over plan to ban ranked choice voting in Dem elections
news.text:
WASHINGTON – Nancy Pelosi’s daughter and Rep. Jamie Raskin are going scorched earth on the Democratic Party for trying to do away with a bizarre style of voting designed to help the underdog candidate and used in New York City.

The Democratic National Committee gathered in Austin Thursday to spend the weekend setting up rules for the next few rounds of elections, including a presidential primary calendar that could favor Kamala Harris and voting on a proposal to ban ranked-choice voting.

The controversy comes amid a Democratic identity crisis. The midterm primaries have exposed the divide between the vocal left wing and the establishment standard-bearers. President Trump and Republicans have taken advantage of the confusion to paint Democrats as led by communists – a critique likely to stay in place through the 2028 election.

Ranked choice voting is a complicated system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference: first, second, third, and so forth.

Raskin, D-Md., said the practice allows the party to be in closer contact with voters, a fear he’s addressed as he travels this summer. 

He wrote on social media he’s getting questions about whether the party “has lost touch with the Democratic grassroots engaged in the fight against Trump and MAGA. I try to assure people that our party leaders are working hard to bolster all the sensational action taking place at the state and local level.”

Advocates say ranked choice voting – used statewide in Maine and Alaska and in large urban areas like Washington DC and New York City – allows for greater choice.

“This effort is not only an attack on the right of Democratic state parties to make their own rules and respond to their own constituents, but it also moves us in exactly the wrong direction in promoting electoral democracy,” Raskin said of attempts to ban the practice.

Christine Pelosi, the daughter of the former speaker and one of 452 voting members of the DNC, vowed to vote against the proposed ban.

“We need radical transparency to restore trust. This ain’t it!,” she wrote on X.

In 2019, New York City voters approved a ballot measure that uses ranked choice voting in certain elections, allowing New Yorkers to rank their top five candidates from first to last choice in all primary and special elections for Mayor, Comptroller, Public Advocate, Borough President and City Council.

But critics complain ranked voting is complicated and expensive. Plus, the candidate with the most votes can lose.

For example, in a 2018 Congressional election in Maine, candidate Bruce Poliquin led in the first round with a plurality – 45.6% – among four candidates. But, without a clear majority winner, ranked choice eliminations were implemented.

About 8% of the vote had gone to candidates who weren’t viable so those were eliminated and the votes shifted to the second choice. Poliquin ended up with 49.5% of the vote, but the winner was Jared Golden with 50.5%.

Proponents argue the system worked – the electorate’s preference was better represented. Opponents say voting should be simpler: those with the most votes win.

Also, in ranked voting, a person’s vote may not count at all. If all of the candidates a voter ranks are eliminated, then their vote is considered “exhausted” and doesn’t go toward any candidate. 

That’s not the only drama happening inside the Austin Hilton where party members are gathered.

Democrats are preparing to finalize their primary calendar for the 2028 presidential election, knocking New Hampshire out of its first-in-the-nation status and elevating South Carolina to the top spot. 

The move could give a boost to former Vice President Harris if she makes another presidential bid. South Carolina’s bloc of black voters would have an outsized influence in naming the Democratic nominee, particularly with no frontrunner aiming for the job.

The calendar sets South Carolina as the first primary on Jan. 22, followed by Nevada on Feb. 1. New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia would round out the early states, voting throughout February.

The party’s Rules and Bylaws committee gave preliminary approval to the calendar last month. Now the entire DNC needs to approve it and the ranked choice voting ban.

Saturday is expected to be the big showdown.
news.summary: Nancy Pelosi’s daughter and Rep. Jamie Raskin are calling out the Democratic Party for trying to do away with a bizarre voting system, used in New York City, designed to help the underdog candidate.

news.title: Former Vikings captain Jack Brewer reacts to Abdul El-Sayed's Senate primary victory in Michigan
news.text: Former Minnesota Vikings captain Jack Brewer described Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senate primary as a "warning shot to America," while praising Michele Tafoya as a credible conservative capable of winning over Minnesota Democrats and independent voters. "It’s good when you see the darkness before you," Brewer said when asked about El-Sayed. "You see exactly what we’re up against as Americans when we have our major cities, major states, with folks like this winning primaries on the verge of having control of populations of that size. "I mean, it’s scary, man," he continued. "It should be a warning shot to America, a warning shot of really where our country is." 2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN Brewer said President Donald Trump’s election victory did not eliminate the political and cultural problems he sees across the country. "When President Trump won the election, it didn’t fix everything," he said. "We’ve got a lot, lot of things to fix. And it’s pretty scary when you start to see these radical leftists starting to gain more and more power across the country." El-Sayed, a physician and former Detroit public health director, narrowly defeated U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary. He will face Republican Mike Rogers in November. El-Sayed ran on a progressive platform that includes Medicare-for-all, higher taxes on billionaire wealth, campaign finance reform and an end to unconditional U.S. military aid to Israel. Brewer acknowledged he had not closely followed El-Sayed before the primary campaign entered its final stages. "Man, I didn’t know much about him to be honest with you," Brewer said. "As the election became closer and closer, you started to hear and see stories and hear the things that he says." Brewer did not identify a particular El-Sayed policy or statement that concerned him. "All I can think about is radical, right? And confused," Brewer said. "It just seems like everything that comes out of his mouth is confusion. "If he’s speaking confusion, that means we have a voting populace that’s confused themselves to be following a guy like this." On another note, Brewer was happy to see Tafoya’s victory in Minnesota’s Republican U.S. Senate primary. El-Sayed’s victory occurred in Michigan, not Minnesota. He is not running against Tafoya. The two races were discussed together as examples of the broader national battle between progressive and conservative candidates in the 2026 midterms. "I was very happy," he said. "Michele Tafoya, who’s a friend and someone that I highly, highly respect, it’s good to see grounded conservative voices stepping up in that state." Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter, won the Republican primary with 52.07% of the vote. Former Navy SEAL Adam Schwarze finished second with 23.96%, while former NBA player Royce White placed third with 11.15%, according to unofficial results from the Minnesota secretary of state. Tafoya will face Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who defeated U.S. Rep. Angie Craig in the DFL primary. "To see someone like herself, and someone that has a name and credibility, is important, especially being a Republican," Brewer said. "You have the cards stacked against you in a lot of ways in a state like Minnesota." No Republican has won a statewide election in Minnesota since 2006. Kamala Harris carried the state in the 2024 presidential election with 50.92% of the vote, compared with Trump’s 46.68%. Despite that history, Brewer predicted Tafoya could build a coalition extending beyond the Republican base. "I think she has a chance to bring over enough Democratic voters and independents to win that election," he said. "So, I’m praying for her." Former NBA player Royce White, who unsuccessfully challenged Tafoya in the Republican primary, also recently announced his plans to declare for the 2027 WNBA Draft. Brewer said he had met White several times and respected his effort to challenge the WNBA’s approach to transgender eligibility. THE WNBA HAS LIMITED OPTIONS AFTER TWO MEN DECLARED FOR THE DRAFT, AND THOSE OPTIONS AREN'T GREAT "I’ve met Royce on a couple occasions," Brewer said. "A lot of respect for him." White and former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom have announced plans to seek entry into the 2027 WNBA Draft. Their announcements are intended to test — or protest —t he league’s eligibility rules by claiming that they identify as women for professional basketball purposes. "I think what he’s doing and Enes is doing is they’re trying to stand up for women," Brewer said. The league has not declared White or Freedom eligible. It said this week there were "no immediate eligibility matters" affecting the WNBA and denounced what it called bad-faith attempts to use the subject to demean or marginalize others. The WNBA has not adopted a publicly available policy saying that surgery qualifies an athlete for the league. Medical organizations also note that transgender identity does not require surgery and that many transgender people never seek surgical treatment. Message to Vikings fans: ‘Enough is enough’ Asked what he would tell Vikings fans before the midterm elections, Brewer urged them to reject Minnesota’s current political leadership. "Stop supporting foolishness," he said. "Enough is enough." Brewer pointed to his own history in the state. He attended the University of Minnesota before playing for the Vikings and three other NFL teams. "I lived in Minnesota for a long time," he said. "I grew up a Vikings fan before I even got a chance to go play there. I went to the University of Minnesota, some of the greatest years of my life. "People have common sense in Minnesota," Brewer continued. "My message to Minnesota is use the common sense that you have. "Stop letting these people that have mental health issues represent you," he said. "You have people that are psychologically not there, and you’re allowing them to represent the state of Minnesota." Brewer did not identify which officeholders he meant or provide evidence supporting that characterization. At the same time, he praised Vikings fans as some of the most welcoming people he encountered during his professional football career. "I played for four NFL teams, and there is nothing like a Minnesota Vikings fan," Brewer said. "These people will have you at home at their dinner table. They will cook for you. They’re the most hospitable people in the world, the nicest, most purest people in the world. "And right now they’re being made a mockery of by the woke left," he added. "I wouldn’t even call them progressive, because they’re not progressive. There’s nothing about progress associated with these leftists. They’ve lost their minds." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Brewer is a prominent Trump ally. He serves as chair of Opportunity Now and vice chair of the Center for 1776 at the America First Policy Institute, a conservative organization closely aligned with the Trump administration.

news.title: Dems turn on Gavin Newsom in Michigan as his visit is brutally panned
news.text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom made the trek to Michigan in his effort to help Democrats retake power in Washington, but that trip seems to have landed with a thud with some would-be allies in his expected presidential bid, according to an on-the-ground report.

One key Dem power broker sniped that she “did not get a call” from the globetrotting gov and another took a veiled swipe at Newsom’s aggressive auto regulations, telling a Politico reporter: “I’m a car girl.” 

The Democratic governor is widely expected to run for the White House in 2028, and Michigan is a key early battleground on the primary calendar. 

Newsom spent time this week in campaigning for down-ballot Democrats in the midwest state, including a meetup with far-left U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, visits to a black church and barbeque event, and a canvassing speech for statehouse Democrats.

But the week was also marred by botched meetings and fundraisers, Politico reported.

Newsom apparently did not meet with Virgie Rollins, the influential chair for the Democratic National Committee’s Black Caucus, despite a liaison reportedly inviting Rollins to a chat.

“Every Democratic president that has won an election has been in my house,” Rollins said. “I did not hear from him. I did not get a call.”

State powerbroker Rep. Debbie Dingell also told Politico that she didn’t hear from Newsom.

“I didn’t hear from the governor. I didn’t expect to: I’m a car girl,” she said, apparently referring to California’s push for fuel emission standards that disproportionately affect the Detroit-heavy car industry.

Newsom attempted to arrange a meeting with Shawn Fain, the United Auto Workers’ president and a key labor figure, but that failed to happen, sources told Politico.

Two fundraisers were also cancelled. Newsom withdrew from one with state attorney general nominee Eli Savit after he found out fundraising host Kelly Neumann, who’s made controversial remarks, would be part of it.

Another event for statehouse Democrats was derailed, with the hosts citing a “small donor base.”

Ultimately, one insider told Politico that Newsom’s trip was just a “B-minus.”

Newsom’s team has portrayed his visit as a success and also promised to schedule meet-ups with some of the people whom he didn’t meet with, such as Rollins. They’ve noted his packed schedule where he met with many Michigan figures, such as Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin.

“Safe to say Michigan Democrats were excited by the opportunity to meet Gavin Newsom,” one of his communications staffers posted on X with video of one of his events.

Newsom’s last known visit to Michigan was July 4, 2024, to campaign for then-President Joe Biden in South Haven. While the trip explicitly was to simply help Michigan Democrats, observers note the obvious political calculations.

“Newsom is clearly taking every opportunity to build relationships here in Michigan,” David Dulio, a political science professor at Oakland University, told the Detroit News. 

“The importance of our state in the presidential contest means it has to be at or near the top of his list of priorities for collecting political chits that he can then cash in when he needs help,” he said.

Newsom, still deemed a potential heavyweight contender, may need all the help he can get. 

Several presidential polls have shown him trailing behind another California hopeful: former Vice President Kamala Harris.
news.summary: The on-the-ground reviews of Newsom’s trip are mixed, Michigan Democrats said.
news.author: Titus Wu

news.title: At the Races: Entering the Florida fray
news.text:
Welcome to At the Races! Each week we bring you news and analysis from the CQ Roll Call campaign team. Know someone who’d like to get this newsletter? They can subscribe here.

Editor's note: Tuesday's newsletter was mistakenly sent again on Wednesday. The version below has the latest information.

By Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari

This week’s primaries in Wisconsin and Minnesota brought mixed results for the Democratic Party’s left flank. 

While progressive Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan decisively won the primary for her state’s open Senate seat, Francesca Hong, the Wisconsin assemblywoman and self-described democratic socialist, narrowly lost her gubernatorial bid to the more moderate Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley. 

The results suggest that support for progressives can still vary from place to place and that individual candidates and their operations play a significant role. And while several races this year have shown Democrats’ preference for a Washington outsider, incumbents have held on across the country.

That’s what Florida Rep. Jared Moskowitz is hoping to do Tuesday against activist Oliver Larkin in one of the final tests of a Democratic incumbent being challenged from the left this primary season. 

That test is coming in South Florida’s newly redrawn 25th District, which Donald Trump would have carried by 9 points in 2024. A quarter of the district’s population is Jewish, while another quarter is Hispanic. Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales rates the race a Toss-up. 

Larkin said progressive wins elsewhere have inspired his supporters, and he’s counting on a robust field operation to win over undecided voters in the campaign’s final days.

“Democrats are not really buying the electability argument that we need to moderate or kind of split the difference between Republican and Democratic points of view on issues,” Larkin, a self-described “proud Democratic Socialist,” said in an interview Wednesday. “What we’re seeing in these states all across the country is that Democrats are really ready to not just be the anti-Trump party, they want an affirmative vision for which side the Democratic Party is on.”

But Larkin’s campaign hasn’t won endorsements from national progressive figures like Bernie Sanders or Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who’ve backed successful primary challengers this year, although he’s set to campaign Friday with Michigan Rep. Rashida Tlaib. He’s also significantly trailed Moskowitz in fundraising, according to the latest federal filings. While most outside spending in the district has been on the Republican side, the center-left New Democrat Majority dropped $250,000 earlier this month on ads to support Moskowitz.

It’s not clear how Larkin’s views on Israel will play in a district with one of the largest Jewish constituencies in the country. He has called for an end to U.S. military aid to Israel, and the Miami Herald editorial board recently criticized him for describing himself as “anti-Zionist.” 

Moskowitz, who is Jewish, has reportedly avoided engaging with his primary rival, accusing him in an interview last month of “running against me solely on my religion.” The congressman declined to comment through a spokesman for this report.

Starting gate

Primary night recap: In addition to the statewide races in Minnesota and Wisconsin on Tuesday, voters picked nominees for a handful of key House races. In Wisconsin, Rebecca Cooke heads to a rematch against GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden in the 3rd District, while in the 7th District, Republican Michael Alfonso, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s son-in-law, is likely to succeed Rep. Tom Tiffany, who won the Republican nomination for governor. And in Minnesota, former state Sen. Matt Little won the Democratic nod to succeed Rep. Angie Craig in the 2nd District. 

Another Palmetto State sprint: South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham will face off against Rep. Ralph Norman in the Aug. 25 Republican special primary runoff to replace her late brother, Lindsey Graham, on the November ballot.

Then there were seven: Connecticut Rep. John B. Larson this week joined six other House Democrats from blue districts who’ve lost primaries this year. But unlike many of the other contests, the race between Larson, 78, and former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, 47, broke along generational, not ideological, lines. And in Hawaii, moderate Democratic Rep. Ed Case, 73, bucked the trend by handily turning back a primary challenge from state Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole, 43. 

Eleventh-hour replacement in NC11: The Republican committee in North Carolina’s 11th District has selected state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom to replace embattled Rep. Chuck Edwards as the party’s nominee. Balkcom will face Democrat Jamie Ager in November.

Seeing blue: The DCCC added ironworker Brian Poindexter of Ohio and former special victims prosecutor Christina Hines of Michigan to its “Red to Blue” program, which offers additional resources to promising recruits seeking to win GOP-held seats.

RIP: Former Georgia Rep. Ben Jones, best known for playing friendly mechanic “Crazy” Cooter on “The Dukes of Hazard,” died Sunday at the age of 84. Our colleague Nick Eskow has more.

Ad watch: New Hampshire's John E. Sununu still has a Republican Senate primary to win next month, but that’s not stopping Rep. Chris Pappas, the likely Democratic nominee, from running an attack ad against him.

2028 incoming: 314 Action Fund, which supports candidates with science and medical backgrounds and is becoming a major spender in Democratic politics, is urging Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly to run for president.

Tax messaging: American Action Network, the nonprofit arm of the Congressional Leadership Fund, has announced a $22 million ad campaign that touts “no tax on tips” and other components of the sprawling tax and spending measure Republicans approved last year. The ads are set to run across 41 House districts.

Targeting swing voters: The conservative super PAC Americans for Prosperity Action is kicking off a $5.6 million national advertising campaign in seven Senate battlegrounds. The effort includes a seven-figure ad buy supporting North Carolina Republican Michael Whatley aimed at winning over swing voters, according to The News & Observer.

Democratic endorsements: Voting rights group Defend the Vote is backing several House candidates, including Mike McGuire, Richard Pan and Randy Villegas in California; Manny Rutinel in Colorado; Bale Dalton in Florida; Jasmine Clark in Georgia; Zach Dembo in Kentucky; Jeremy Moss in Michigan; Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania; and Chaz Molder in Tennessee. The moderate Blue Dog PAC is also endorsing Dembo, as well as Brian Poindexter in Ohio, JoAnna Mendoza in Arizona, Leela Gray in Florida, Sam Forstag in Montana and Blake Gendebien in New York.

#LA05: Louisiana state Sen. Blake Miguez, who had Trump’s endorsement in his bid to succeed Senate nominee Julia Letlow in the 5th District, switched to the redrawn 6th District before the candidate filing deadline last week. Democratic incumbent Cleo Fields is vacating the seat for a state Senate run after state Republicans redrew it as a deep-red bastion. 

#MIGOV: Michigan Rep. John James, the Republican nominee for governor, named state Rep. Jay DeBoyer as his running mate. James will next face Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who is yet to name her ticket mate.

Nathan's notes

The Ohio and Michigan Senate delegations could be in for some awkwardness next year if Sherrod Brown and Mike Rogers are elected this fall, writes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections. That’s because they would then serve with senators who defeated them previously.

It’s not that rare a phenomenon, Nathan observes, with more than a dozen such odd Senate pairs serving in recent memory.

What we're reading

Untangling a web: Inside Elections’ Jacob Rubashkin delves into the world of left-leaning dark-money groups funding independent candidates in Republican territory. According to Rubashkin, the most expensive effort has been in Montana, where Seth Bodnar, a former Green Beret and erstwhile president of the University of Montana, is running as an independent in a three-way race against Republican Kurt Alme and Democrat Alani Bankhead.

#MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom sees a rare opportunity to flip a Mississippi seat this year, The Associated Press reports, as his party looks to expand the Senate map. But while the state has a larger share of Black voters than any other state, Republicans largely scoff at the notion that incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith may be vulnerable. 

San Francisco fault line: Both Democrats running for the House seat of retiring former Speaker Nancy Pelosi share progressive views on most topics. But San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan and state Sen. Scott Wiener are divided on housing policy, a key issue in an area where the median rent for a one-bedroom apartment has surpassed $4,000, CalMatters found.

A bridge too far: Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee is fighting for his political survival against fellow Democrat Helena Foulkes. McKee is among the nation’s most unpopular governors and a key reason for that is voter anger over the partially closed Washington Bridge. “Almost everybody says the bridge is the No. 1 issue in the race and voters’ perception of McKee’s tenure,’’ Politico writes.

The count: 19

That's the maximum number of states and territories that could have a former member of Congress serving as governor by early next year. 

Six states – Alabama, Arizona, California, Michigan, Tennessee and Wisconsin – and the U.S. Virgin Islands have an opportunity this fall to elect a governor with congressional experience to succeed one without. 

Four states currently have term-limited former lawmakers in their governor’s mansions and could elect successors with similar backgrounds. It’s virtually guaranteed to happen in Florida, where Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly are favored to face off in November. Minnesota and New Mexico are likely to elect Democrats Amy Klobuchar and Deb Haaland as their respective next governors. And former GOP Rep. Greg Lopez is running a long-shot independent bid in Colorado. 

Two governors seeking reelection this year are former members themselves — New Hampshire Republican Kelly Ayotte and New York Democrat Kathy Hochul. 

Meanwhile, six states and one territory have former members as governors who aren’t up for reelection in November — Indiana, Louisiana, Montana, New Jersey, North Dakota, Virginia and Puerto Rico. 

And one state has a term-limited governor — former Ohio Sen. and Rep. Mike DeWine — who will be succeeded by someone who hasn’t represented the state in Washington.

– By Roll Call’s Ryan Kelly

Key race: #AKSEN

Candidates: Sixteen candidates are competing in Tuesday’s all-party primary, with the top four finishers moving on to the November ballot. Two-term Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan is locked in a close race with Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola. Complicating the task for Sullivan: the entrance of Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher and a Republican Trump critic. Sen. Sullivan and his supporters sought to remove him from the ballot, calling his candidacy a scheme by Democrats to confuse voters and give Peltola an edge. Last month, the state Supreme Court ruled that the other Sullivan could remain, though he won’t be identified as a Republican.

Why it matters: Democrats have won exactly one Senate election in Alaska in the past five decades, and that was against a Republican who had just been convicted on corruption charges. But the party landed a prize recruit in Peltola, a moderate who lost her at-large House seat by 2 points in 2024, even as Trump was carrying the state by 13 points. 

Cash dash: Peltola has consistently outraised the incumbent, bringing in $18.5 million to his $11.8 million through July 29, though Sullivan had $7.3 million banked to Peltola’s $4.6 million. Both candidates are getting plenty of outside help: Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing Senate Republicans, recently announced that it would spend an additional $2 million to boost Sullivan, bringing its total commitment in The Last Frontier to $17 million. Meanwhile the group’s Democratic counterpart, Senate Majority PAC, has already reserved $10 million in ads to back Peltola. In the run-up to the primary, a number of pop-up super PACs whose donors are not yet public have begun running ads seeking to boost some of the lesser-known candidates on the ballot, the Alaska Beacon reports. 

Backers: Before the 2024 election, Peltola would not say whether she would vote for Kamala Harris. But this year, she picked up Harris’ endorsement. (In a twist, Peltola’s campaign unveiled a new ad this week slamming Sullivan for voting for two Biden administration nominees.) Sullivan has Trump’s endorsement and the backing of the National Rifle Association and several veterans and labor groups.

What they’re saying: Peltola, the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress, supports abortion rights and other mainstream Democratic positions. But she has broken with the party over gun policy, and her campaign slogan – “fish, family, freedom – reflects her independent streak. In a state where the cost of living outpaces the national average, she has focused on affordability concerns. Sullivan and his GOP allies have cast Peltola as a liberal, trying to tie her to her party’s democratic socialists. While Sullivan has generally backed the president, he voted for a measure that sought to ban funding for the White House ballroom that wasn’t approved by Congress and against Trump’s plan to establish a compensation fund for people he views as victims of political prosecution.

Terrain: A state as red as Alaska should be safe GOP territory, but Peltola’s fundraising prowess, confusion over the two Dan Sullivans and a midterm environment that favors Democrats have combined to put the Senate seat in play. Inside Elections rates the race Lean Republican.

Wild card: Under the state’s ranked choice voting system, voters arrange candidates in order of preference. If the leader does not get more than 50 percent in the first tally, the fourth-place finisher is eliminated and his or her votes are added to the voters’ second choice. The process may be repeated until one candidate gets a majority. The system helped Peltola notch her first House win in 2022, when she emerged from a crowded primary field of 48 candidates, including Republican former Gov. Sarah Palin, to win a special election following Republican Rep. Don Young’s death.

Alaska, Florida and Wyoming are holding primaries on Tuesday. The same day, voters in California’s 14th District will elect a successor to disgraced former Rep. Eric Swalwell.

news.title: Hasan Piker is becoming the 'face of the progressive movement,' former Democratic operative warns
news.text: Controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker has found himself at the center of a debate about the direction of the Democratic Party and generations of voters to come. However, recently on his stream, which he does for hours every day, the far-left commentator has claimed the media is making him out to have more influence than he actually does. Evan Barker, author of "Nothing Left: Confessions Of A Democratic Operative," disagrees with Piker's analysis of his own popularity — he has more than 3 million followers on Twitch and millions more across other social media accounts — pointing to the increasing number of candidates who have invited him to campaign with them. "Why would these candidates have this desire to bring him into their state, to campaign alongside him if he wasn't influential, to hold press junkets with him, to invite him to barbecues? Like, why would they be doing that if he didn't have influence? Like, clearly, he does," Barker told Fox News Digital. Barker is no stranger to Democratic politics. She raised tens of millions of dollars for Democratic candidates, campaigned for Hillary Clinton and worked for candidates backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. EX-DEM OPERATIVE DETAILS 'NEW DONOR ESTABLISHMENT' BEHIND MAMDANI-ERA PROGRESSIVES: 'NOT FROM THE GRASSROOTS' Barker eventually broke with the party in 2024, a journey she details in her new book. She told Fox News Digital that Democrats are "testing their limits with the popularity" in areas of the country that aren't deep blue, especially when campaigning with Piker. "It's one thing to appear on somebody's podcast, it's another to have them come campaign for you," she said. Piker's hours-long stream primarily focuses on politics. He has backed several candidates in the 2026 cycle, including Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong. While El-Sayed won his primary race, Hong lost to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who has since said he was not planning on campaigning with Piker. Piker's long history of incendiary and far-left rhetoric has made him an easy target for Republicans. From his retracted comments about saying the U.S. "deserved" 9/11, to his praise of Chinese dictator Mao Zedong, and the hours of talking he does every day, there's no shortage of comments for which Piker and his allies could be held to account. When asked what she would tell candidates who are thinking about campaigning with the Twitch streamer, Barker told Fox News Digital that she would advise against it. "I would say that the juice isn't worth the squeeze," she said. "Yeah, you're trying to appeal to younger voters, you're trying to drive out your base, but how do you win a general election aligning with him?" DEMOCRAT ESTABLISHMENT STRIKES BACK AS SOCIALIST CANDIDATE DOWNED IN BATTLEGROUND PRIMARY While Barker has expressed skepticism about Piker, she said she often hears those on the left defend their relationship with the streamer by comparing him to another media personality: Joe Rogan. During the 2024 campaign cycle, then-Vice President Kamala Harris was criticized for not appearing on Rogan's widely followed podcast while running for president, particularly after both now-Vice President JD Vance and now-President Donald Trump sat for interviews with him. Some have made the case that Piker could serve as an alternative to Rogan, but Barker disagrees. "Hasan Piker is not at all like Joe Rogan, actually. So, the charm of Joe Rogan, what makes his show so powerful, is that he talks about politics sometimes. Politics is sometimes peppered into his conversations, but by and large, the majority of the time, he's not talking about politics," she said. "Whereas Hasan Piker, that's pretty much all he talks about." She also noted that some of Piker's rhetoric that appeals to younger voters might not resonate with larger populations in parts of the country that are not deep blue. "At the end of the day, I would remind these progressive candidates, it's not just about pleasing your staff, it's not just about pleasing, you know, the young people that are in this movement. If you want to win places like Wisconsin, if you want to win places like Michigan, you have to be patriotic," she said. "The Rust Belt is filled with hardworking patriotic Americans who don't feel the way that Hasan Piker does." WISCONSIN DEMOCRATIC VOTERS CHALK SOCIALIST FRANCESCA HONG'S STUNNING LOSS UP TO ELECTABILITY CONCERNS As Democrats weigh the consequences of backlash for campaigning with Piker against the access to younger voters that he brings, Barker says the streamer is quickly becoming well known offline as well. She argued that Piker is "probably the biggest podcaster, live streamer" that the Democrats have at their disposal. "He's quickly becoming a household name. He's quickly becoming the face of the progressive movement," she said. Barker acknowledged that some progressives may not be "comfortable" with Piker as a de facto leader, calling his rise a "monster that they've created themselves." She also compared the current moment to previous shifts within the progressive movement, arguing that figures and ideas once embraced by the left are later dismissed as excesses of an earlier era. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Barker pointed specifically to recent discussions of "Woke 1" after Ocasio-Cortez's invocation of the term last week, arguing that Democrats have yet to reckon with the consequences of that period around 2020, which was marked by a surge in racial identity politics and progressive groupthink. "People's lives were ruined because of 'woke 1.' It wasn't just some mass delusion or mass hysteria that we all went through... It pushed people away from Democratic politics," she said. Barker argued that Democrats' continued willingness to align with figures like Piker shows the party has yet to move beyond that period. "I think that there needs to be a true reckoning in the progressive movement and in the Democratic Party for people to really be able to heal and move on from this," she said. news.summary: Hasan Piker is becoming the face of the progressive movement, says former Democratic operative Evan Barker, who warns candidates against working with him.

news.title: Haitians in Ohio who lost protected status get ankle monitors instead of ICE detention
news.text: Haitians living in Ohio who’ve lost their protected status are increasingly getting ankle monitors instead of being detained by immigration officers, attorneys say. ICE has been alerting Haitians to appear in person at check-ins, where they are given ankle monitors to track their whereabouts until an immigration judge can decide whether they may have a legitimate reason to remain in the country, such as an asylum claim, according to the lawyers. The decision is often made over a lack of detention space for more than 300,000 Haitians who lost Temporary Protected Status after a Supreme Court decision in June, a senior Department of Homeland Security official said. “We were really worried that this was going to be a mass enforcement, mass detention operation,” said Katie Kersh, an immigration attorney who represents Haitian clients as part of her work at the Ohio-based law firm Advocates for Basic Legal Equality. Instead, Kersh said, several of her clients recently received ICE letters mandating the in-person check-ins. “And so we went,” she said. People were arrested but not detained for the long term. “They all have these ankle monitors and they’re not allowed to travel outside of a 75-mile radius from their home.” DHS declined to comment on the ankle monitors. “DHS does not discuss ongoing or future operations,” a spokesperson said in an emailed statement. “What we would say now is it’s closing time, which means you don’t have to go home, but you can’t stay here.” It is the latest policy shift since DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin took over in March that could draw President Donald Trump’s ire. Last month, Mullin ran afoul of President Donald Trump when he announced a halt on vehicle pursuits by ICE after fatal shootings. The ankle monitors and other trackers allow immigrants to continue to live in the U.S. while their cases play out. The program was bolstered under the Biden administration but Trump’s immigration policy architect, Stephen Miller, prefers holding immigrants in detention. A senior administration official and DHS official told NBC News recently there was growing tension between the White House and Mullin, this administration’s second Homeland Security secretary, though the president does not appear to be preparing to oust him. Temporary Protected Status is a humanitarian program created by Congress that allows people from countries ravaged by war, natural disasters or other extreme circumstances to come and live and work in the United States temporarily. In June, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to end the protections for more than 300,000 Haitians who came to the country following the 2010 earthquake, and the more than 50,000 Syrians who came when the civil war broke out in their country in 2015. Previous administrations and lower courts had determined the conditions in both of those countries were still too dire to end protections against deportations there. The order has sowed confusion among business owners who employ Haitians, and employees who have been unsure when or how they should show up to work. The senior DHS official said it would be impossible to hold the more than 300,000 Haitians in the U.S. who lost their protected status in ICE detention. ICE currently is holding about 65,000 immigrants in detention facilities across the country, until a judge can hear their case. NBC has reported ICE is working to open new detention facilities. Last month, Mullin instructed ICE officers to pause vehicle stops following two fatal shootings of men in vehicles, but the policy was quickly overturned by Trump. Mullin had not run the pause by the White House, NBC News reported, citing a senior administration official. Trump has repeatedly focused on Haitian immigrants in the United States. On the campaign trail in 2024, Trump and his running mate, Vice President JD Vance lent credence to false rumors that began on social media that a Haitian immigrant in Springfield, Ohio, had eaten a cat. “In Springfield, the people that came in, they’re eating the dogs … they’re eating the cats,” Trump said in a September 2024 debate with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. The Facebook post that sparked the rumor was later debunked, but Trump’s rhetoric fired up immigration hard-liners who supported him in the election.
news.author: Julia Ainsley,Nathan Gonzalez

news.title: AOC overtakes Rubio in 2028 presidential Polymarket odds
news.text:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) has overtaken Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the latest 2028 presidential odds on prediction market platform Polymarket, adding to speculation that the progressive New York Democrat could emerge as an early favorite for the party’s nomination.

Ocasio-Cortez and Rubio have both been floated as possible contenders for their respective parties’ 2028 presidential nominations, though both have sought to keep the focus on the 2026 midterm elections.

Ocasio-Cortez’s rise in the prediction markets comes as she faces growing speculation about a possible presidential bid. Vice President JD Vance said in June that he believes Ocasio-Cortez will be the leading Democratic candidate in 2028.

“I think it’s got to be AOC. I know that’s probably conventional wisdom,” Vance said during an interview on The Michael Knowles Show. Ocasio-Cortez has not ruled out a presidential campaign, though she has repeatedly emphasized that she is focused on the midterm elections.

“I’m focused on winning the midterms. I’m running for Congress right now,” Ocasio-Cortez told ABC’s This Week last week when asked whether she plans to run for president in two years.

“I haven’t ruled out the possibility. And I’m very humbled to the tremendous amount of support out there,” she added.

Other Democrats being floated as possible 2028 contenders include Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-CA), Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), former Vice President Kamala Harris, and former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel.

Recent polling has also shown Ocasio-Cortez emerging as a formidable possible contender. A poll of likely New Hampshire Democratic primary voters conducted last month found 22% would support Ocasio-Cortez if the primary were held today, narrowly edging former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg at 21%.

RealClearPolitics’s polling aggregate, however, currently shows Harris leading the Democratic field by 12 points, underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the early 2028 race.

On the Republican side, Vance and Rubio have emerged as two of the most frequently discussed possible contenders.

A report from the Washington Post alleged that President Donald Trump told donors that “at the end of the day, we need to elect JD.”

Trump denied endorsing Vance shortly after, saying, “I heard about it a little while ago. I think he’s great, but we’re way too early to even be thinking about that”Trump suggested in May that Vance and Rubio could make a “dream team” during a White House event, though he stopped short of endorsing either for president.

ONE YEAR LATER, SOME DC RESIDENTS PRAISE TRUMP’S NATIONAL GUARD DEPLOYMENT

“That does not mean you have my endorsement under any circumstance,” Trump said. “But you know … I think it sounds like presidential candidate and vice presidential candidate.”

While speculation over the 2028 field continues to grow, party leaders in both parties remain largely focused on the 2026 midterm elections before making decisions about the next presidential race.

news.title: EXCLUSIVE: GOA's Erich Pratt Reminds Voters How Good Trump Has Been for 2A Rights
news.text:
Gun Owners of America’s Erich Pratt spoke exclusively to Breitbart News Thursday, describing the demise of NFA suppressor registration as just the latest result of President Trump’s pro-Second Amendment stance.

On August 5, 2026, Breitbart News reported that U.S. District Judge James Wesley Hendrix ruled against National Firearms Act (NFA) registration requirements in Jensen v. ATF. This opened the door for plaintiffs in the case–including those in a consolidated case–to transfer suppressors and short barrel rifles and shotguns without complying with NFA registration requirements.

Caveat: Judge Hendrix allowed the government a seven-day window in which to appeal his ruling before allowing it to take effect. This meant that, barring appeal, it would take effect August 13, 2026. The DOJ did not appeal during the seven-day window and shortly after midnight August 13, 2026, the Silencer Shop and Gun Owners of America celebrated the “first lawful, unregistered suppressor transfer since June 26th, 1934.”

Pratt addressed these developments, saying, “Trump has shown real leadership on this NFA issue. He pushed the One Big Beautiful Bill into law last year, I mean he pushed it hard. And that bill reduced the federal tax on suppressors and short barrel rifles and shotguns to zero dollars. And Trump praised the elimination of the NFA taxes.”

He continued, “Then, on Wednesday of this week, he told Congressman Andrew Clyde (R) he had instructed the DOJ not to appeal the Jensen v. ATF decision.”

“Oh, by the way, the judge who issued the ruling against NFA registration is a Trump-appointed judge, so from beginning to end, we are reminded again that elections matter and have consequences,” he added. “All these wins we have experienced would not have happened under a Kamala Harris administration.”

AWR Hawkins is an award-winning Second Amendment columnist for Breitbart News and the writer/curator of Down Range with AWR Hawkins, a weekly newsletter focused on all things Second Amendment, also for Breitbart News. He is the political analyst for Armed American Radio and the director of global marketing for Lone Star Hunts. He holds a PhD in Military History with a focus on the Vietnam War (brown water navy), U.S. Navy since Inception, the Civil War, and Early Modern Europe. He enjoys reading Philosophy and novels by Jack Carr and Nelson DeMille. He is a lever action man in an AR-15 world. Follow him on X: @awrhawkins. You can sign up to get Down Range at breitbart.com/downrange. Reach him directly at awrhawkins@breitbart.com.

news.title: One of the most controversial campaign ads of 2026 leads to new lawsuit
news.text:
In the current Congress, the number of House Republicans willing to break party ranks on key issues has been vanishingly small, but Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania tends to be one of them, and there’s no great mystery as to why.

The GOP congressman represents a district that supported Barack Obama, Joe Biden and Gov. Josh Shapiro, among other Democrats. He’s also one of only three House Republicans running for re-election in a district Kamala Harris won. With this in mind, Fitzpatrick understands that it’s in his electoral interest to maintain at least some distance from his party’s far-right agenda.

But away from Capitol Hill, Fitzpatrick’s tactics are anything but “moderate.”

Hoping to undermine Democrat Bob Harvie, a member of the Bucks County Board of Commissioners, Fitzpatrick’s political operation has run attack ads telling local voters that his rival is “under FBI investigation.”

The trouble is that there’s nothing to suggest Harvie is, or ever was, facing any FBI scrutiny. He testified before a grand jury as a witness five years ago — in a case that never led to charges against anyone — and according to the Democrat’s lawyers, he is not now and has never been the subject of any criminal investigation.

Given the enormous difference between testifying in a case and being the defendant in a case, Harvie’s lawyers sent Fitzpatrick’s campaign a cease-and-desist letter last month, insisting that the ads are categorically false and defamatory. The Republican congressman and his team not only ignored the letter, Fitzpatrick practically dared Harvie to file a lawsuit.

“They said they were going to file a lawsuit. And guess what? Guess what? They didn’t file a lawsuit,” Fitzpatrick said last month.

They’ve now filed a lawsuit. HuffPost reported:

Last week, Harvie actually sued. He filed a defamation case against Defending America PAC [a political action committee aligned with Fitzpatrick] and Chris Pack, a Republican consultant, accusing them of “repeatedly and recklessly publishing false and defamatory statements imputing criminal conduct that go beyond the bounds even of a highly contested political campaign.”

To date, Fitzpatrick, his campaign team, his consultant or the PAC supporting his candidacy have not commented on the Democrat’s lawsuit. Watch this space.

news.title: The right has a blind spot about young women
news.text:
Massachusetts Democratic Gov. Maura Healey, a lesbian who claims to be Catholic, signed legislation this week liberalizing abortion while surrounded by progressive women celebrating the right to murder their healthy babies up till birth. To conservatives who rightly regard late-term abortion as the killing of a viable child, the scene was grotesque.

It also illustrated a political asymmetry conservatives rarely discuss.

A civilization where men and women are constantly at odds with each other is doomed.

Endless ink has been spilled and countless podcasts recorded about the radicalization of young men on the right. Almost nobody in conservative media wants to address the equally serious radicalization of young women toward the progressive left.

There has been plenty of controversy in conservative circles about young men embracing nihilistic or extremist politics online. Rod Dreher, among others, has warned about young conservative men drifting toward figures such as Nick Fuentes and adopting a politics of resentment and despair.

That’s fine as far as it goes, but it does not answer the larger question. Even if Dreher is right about one cohort of men, it does not follow that young men are uniquely radicalized, or even that they represent the larger political problem. Conservatives should be capable of noticing more than one trend at a time. And the trend among women is impossible to ignore.

Kamala Harris received 53% of the female vote in 2024, while Joe Biden received 54% in 2020. Women are substantially more supportive than men of legal abortion. They are also more likely to regard changing one’s gender as morally acceptable and more likely to say society has not done enough to accommodate transgender people.

The same divide appears on immigration. Women are more likely to support amnesty, oppose ICE deportations, and favor extending legal protections to illegal immigrants.

The divide extends beyond electoral politics. Young women are less likely than young men to say they want children and less likely to prioritize family over professional goals. They are also less likely to express a positive view of capitalism.

None of this means women are a political monolith. Marriage changes voting behavior dramatically. Married women are far more likely to vote Republican and hold traditional views on family and gender.

Race also plays a part.

Ripping on liberal white women is practically a conservative pastime, partly because “white” makes them culturally safe targets. But the voting data complicate the caricature. A majority of white women voted for Trump in 2024, while much smaller shares of Hispanic, Asian, Jewish, and black women did so.

RELATED: Stop ‘owning the libs’ and start owning institutions

 Blaze Media Illustration 

White women are hardly a uniformly conservative bloc. But they are not the most progressive female constituency either.

Despite the mountain of evidence that females are far more left wing, there will be no books about the dangerous trend of radicalization among young women. There will be plenty of cable-news segments about how social media is poisoning young men. There will be endless concern about podcasts, gaming culture, online masculinity, and the political temptations facing disaffected boys.

Much less energy will be spent asking what TikTok, universities, activist institutions, and elite media have done to the minds of young women.

The reason is simple: Young men are a safe target.

Anyone can denounce them with little institutional risk. A broad criticism of female political behavior, by contrast, can quickly become a career problem. That taboo exists on the right almost as surely as it does on a college campus.

It must be said that this is not an exercise in blanket condemnation of women. The conservative movement is filled with passionate, caring, godly mothers, wives, daughters, and single women who genuinely support the fight for the future of the United States.

A civilization where men and women are constantly at odds with each other is doomed. Breaking men and women out of loving families and turning them into political blocs to be catered to is disastrous for the health of the nation.

South Korea provides a warning about where gender war can lead. Its political divide between young men and women has grown exceptionally wide, with the sexes increasingly supporting very different parties and organizing around competing political identities.

South Korea also has one of the lowest fertility rates in the world. That does not prove the political gender divide caused the fertility collapse; housing costs, work culture, marriage patterns, and other factors have played a role. But a society in which men and women increasingly regard one another as political adversaries will have a harder time persuading them to marry, form families, and raise children together.

North Korea, despite being totalitarian and impoverished, has a higher fertility rate than the South. No sane person would therefore prefer living under a communist mad man. The comparison simply shows that prosperity alone cannot guarantee family formation. A wealthy society can still undermine itself if men and women cease to see one another as partners in a common project.

RELATED: Conservatives are blowing the easiest political win in America

 Blaze Media Illustration

The basic building block of society is not the individual but the family. In a democracy, when you separate men and women into different constituencies, you fundamentally undermine family formation and create a dangerous antagonism between the sexes.

This is not a call for further politicization. It is a call to recognize the dynamics already playing out in the conservative sphere.

Young men are easy targets, and they should be corrected when they embrace nihilism or extremism. But young women have also shifted sharply left with virtually no comparable attention from the conservative commentariat.

The asymmetry is especially strange because conservatives insist that adults are moral agents responsible for their choices. That principle cannot suddenly disappear when the subject is young women. If progressive politics encourages destructive beliefs about abortion, sex, marriage, family, borders, or economics, conservatives should be willing to say so plainly rather than treating female voters as a protected class.

If conservatives want to be honest about the cultural problems facing the country, they cannot provide moral correction and guidance only to their sons. Their daughters need it too.

We must end the gender wars and encourage unity and family formation in the United States. But doing that will require conservatives to tell some women a phrase they very rarely hear: No.
