news.title: These states will make or break a Senate majority in November
news.text:
Below is a breakdown of the “toss-up,” “lean Democratic,” and “lean Republican” states that will give each party a path to the Senate majority in November.

Toss Up: Alaska

Two-term Sen. Dan Sullivan will defend his seat against former Rep. Mary Peltola. Sullivan’s challenger was the last Democrat to represent Alaska statewide, serving in Alaska’s sole House of Representatives seat from 2023 to 2025.

Sullivan is a reliable conservative, though he has occasionally broken from President Donald Trump’s agenda on topics like the White House ballroom and the Department of Justice’s Anti-Weaponization Fund.

Peltola, meanwhile, has stressed her independent streak as an outdoorswoman and Yup’ik native. She is one of the few Democrats to have received a National Rifle Association endorsement in the past, though the NRA is backing Sullivan this cycle.

Trump won Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024. Yet ranked choice voting, a strong candidate, and a fundraising advantage all give Democrats hope they can flip the seat. Peltola raised $7 million in the second quarter compared to Sullivan’s $2 million, but the GOP senator had $2.3 million more on hand as of late June.

The race also took an unexpected turn when Dan J. Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher, registered for the ballot. Republicans took that Sullivan to court, arguing that his political aspirations were a stunt to confuse voters who intended to vote for the similarly-named senator.

The Alaska Supreme Court greenlit his candidacy, however. Both Sullivans will appear on the ballot for the Aug. 18 nonpartisan primary, with Dan S. Sullivan’s box specifying that he is the incumbent. The top four vote getters will advance to the general election.

Toss Up: Ohio

Longtime Sen. Sherrod Brown is hoping to fight his way back to Capitol Hill. Brown served three terms before losing in 2024 to Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-OH). Now, Brown hopes to serve alongside Moreno.

Brown will face incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R-OH) in November. Husted has a long political record in his home state, having served as Ohio’s Secretary of State and lieutenant governor. The November election will be Husted’s first for the Senate, however. Gov. Mike DeWine (R) appointed him in 2025 to replace then-Sen. J.D. Vance, who resigned to become vice president.

Ohio was formerly a partisan battleground, though the Trump effect has turned it into a reliably Republican state. Trump won Ohio by more than 11 percentage points in 2024, an increase from his 2020 showing in the state. 

Yet Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer recruited a strong candidate in Brown, who has the populist streak and Senate credentials to be a viable option in Ohio.

Given his political background, Brown is no stranger to fundraising. Brown brought in $14.1 million in the second quarter, walloping Husted by $10 million. He finished the quarter with $16.2 million on hand compared to Husted’s $9.4 million.

One factor that will make the Ohio Senate election even more of a nail-biter is Vivek Ramaswamy’s appearance on the top of the ballot. Ramaswamy, a long-shot presidential candidate turned brief Trump adviser, is hoping to succeed DeWine as governor. It remains to be seen whether the conservative firebrand’s campaign propels or pulls back Husted’s candidacy.

Toss Up: Michigan

Michigan’s Senate election is turning from a proxy battle between the Democratic Party’s progressive and institutional wings to a fight between the Republican and Democratic Parties more broadly.

Democrats are fielding 41-year-old progressive Abdul el Sayed. El Sayed has an impressive resume: he spoke before President Bill Clinton at his University of Michigan graduation ceremony and won a Rhodes Scholarship to study public health. He later challenged Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D-MI) in the 2018 gubernatorial primary election, raking in just under a third of the vote.

Not every Democrat is dazzled by him, however. El Sayed only recently emerged from his hotly-contested primary election against Rep. Hailey Stevens (D-MI). Outside groups opposed to el Sayed’s candidacy poured vast sums into the election, including some $32 million in ads from the pro-Israel organization AIPAC. 

El Sayed is the son of Michigan’s large Arab community, which may win him some support in November. Yet his progressive policies may prove out of step with voters in the midwestern swing state that Trump flipped by 1.4 percentage points in 2024.

For their part, major voices in the Democratic Party, including Stevens and Whitmer, quickly coalesced around el Sayed after the election.

El Sayed will face former Rep. Mike Rogers in November. With incumbent Sen. Gary Peters (D-MI) bowing out of reelection, Michigan is a target for national Republicans. Rogers narrowly lost to Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) on the same 2024 ballot that Trump topped, a possible issue with voter enthusiasm. 

Yet the real reason election observers will be watching the Michigan Senate primary is to see whether el Sayed will be able to coalesce the Democratic base, or whether Democrats will lose this critical seat for their Senate majority. 

Toss Up: Maine

Maine, one of the most important pickups for Democrats, has proven a thorn in the party’s side. Democratic presidential candidates have won the popular vote in Maine since 1992, and one of the state’s two senators is an independent who caucuses with the Democrats.

Those factors make the state an obvious Democratic target. Yet a candidate quality scandal embroiled Democrats over the summer, potentially jeopardizing their chances to defeat five-term Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME). 

Gov. Janet Mills (D) and Marine Corps veteran Graham Platner were the two frontrunners for the Democratic nomination. Mills dropped out of the race in April, however, citing financial challenges. That left the race open for Platner, who had previously been a political unknown.

Platner rocketed to national attention through his made-for-social-media campaign style, which national political strategists helped to cultivate. But he also had his fair share of skeletons in his closet, including a Nazi tattoo and sexual assault accusations. The sexual assault scandals ultimately forced Platner to suspend his campaign in July.

Maine Democrats held a nominating contest in which they selected former state Senate President Troy Jackson as Platner’s replacement. Jackson, like Platner, is a populist progressive. Yet Democrats hope that Jackson does not have as big of a target on his back for Collins to exploit in November.

The November contest will test whether Jackson can make up for that lost time, or whether the Platner saga sunk Democratic chances in this pivotal seat.

Lean Democrat: Georgia

There was a period in Georgia politics in which it would have been unthinkable for both senators to be Democrats. That period ended with two January 2021 special elections where Sens. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) and Raphael Warnock (D-GA) both won election.

Warnock defended his seat successfully in 2022. Ossoff now hopes to do the same against Rep. Mike Collins (R-GA), a two-term congressman with a combative social media presence.

Critics have argued that Ossoff only succeeded in 2021 because he appeared on the ballot alongside Warnock, a prominent preacher in the state’s black community. Ossoff, the youngest member of the Senate, reportedly wavered on whether he’d run again because he wanted to spend more time with his wife and two children.

Ossoff has become a darling in the Democratic Party, however, with some pundits floating him as a possible 2028 presidential contender. Ossoff has repeatedly insisted that he isn’t interested in a White House bid.

Ossoff has also proven to be one of the Democratic Party’s most gifted fundraisers. He finished the second quarter with a $42 million war chest, a staggering figure compared to the $2.2 million in Collins’s coiffures. The national GOP has intervened in an attempt to prop Collins up financially, though Ossoff has saturated Georgia with television ads using his campaign cash.

Ossoff has harped on Collins’s relationship to his son-in-law, a white supremacist influencer. Collins, meanwhile, has criticized Ossoff for his hefty out-of-state fundraising. The November election will test whether Collins can overcome a formidable fundraising disadvantage in what has become a perennial swing state.

Lean Democrat: North Carolina

Democrats selected one of the best candidates possible in the North Carolina Senate races. Former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) is a popular moderate, and he is widely expected to succeed outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC) in January.

Cooper is a veteran of the governor’s mansion, the attorney general’s office, and the state legislature. He was elected twice on ballots where Trump won North Carolina, first in 2016 and then in 2020. He has historically been a palatable choice for split-ticket voters, which may be a boon for his campaign in November.

Cooper’s opponent is former Republican National Committee and North Carolina Republican Party Chairman Michael Whatley. The GOP operative has Trump’s backing, which has proven decisive in races across the country.

“He is fantastic at everything he does, and he was certainly great at the RNC where, in the Presidential Election, we won every Swing State, the Popular Vote, and the Electoral College by a landslide!” Trump wrote last year on Truth Social, even before Whatley declared his candidacy. “But I have a mission for my friends in North Carolina, and that is to get Michael Whatley to run for the U.S. Senate.”

Whatley may have Trump’s valuable endorsement, but Cooper is more familiar to North Carolina voters than Whatley, who is still working to increase his name recognition across the state.

Lean Democrat: New Hampshire

As Democrats are doing in Ohio, New Hampshire Republicans are fielding a former senator as their pick to flip a seat held by the other party. Former Sen. John Sununu represented New Hampshire between 2003 and 2009 before losing reelection to Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH).

Shaheen announced last year that she would not seek reelection. Rep. Chris Pappas (D-NH) is all but certain to be the Democratic nominee to replace her, though neither Pappas nor Sununu have won their primary elections yet.

The Sununu family is New Hampshire’s preeminent political dynasty. John’s brother, Chris, served as governor for four two-year terms. Their father, also a John, was governor in the 1980s and then chief of staff to President George H.W. Bush. The family has wide name recognition and deep political connections in the Granite State.

The November election will test that political clout. Though New Hampshire’s margins are closer than many other states, it has reliably fallen into the Democratic column in presidential elections. Vice President Kamala Harris won the state by 2.8 percentage points in 2024.

Voters in New Hampshire have not backed a Republican presidential candidate since 2000. Still, it would not be unprecedented for New Hampshire to send a Republican to the Senate. Gov. Kelly Ayotte (R) represented New Hampshire in the upper chamber until 2017.

Lean Republican: Iowa

Iowa was a swing state that twice backed President Barack Obama, though it has turned red under Trump. Democrats hope that state Rep. Josh Turek, a made-for-politics candidate, will give them a chance to flip this Senate seat.

He was born with spina bifida because of his father’s Agent Orange exposure in Vietnam. He is also a two-time Paralympic gold medalist.

Turek and his opponent, Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-IA), are both vying to replace outgoing Sen. Joni Ernst (R-IA).

Hinson was a broadcast journalist and state legislator before winning election to the House of Representatives in 2020. Her district covers much of southeastern Iowa, including Waterloo and Cedar Falls. The congresswoman received Trump’s coveted endorsement for the Senate seat.

“I know Ashley well, and she is a WINNER! A Loving Wife and Proud Mother of two sons, Ashley is a wonderful person, has ALWAYS delivered for Iowa, and will continue doing so in the United States Senate,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last year.

Hinson is the clear frontrunner in Iowa, which Trump won by more than 13 percentage points in 2024. Democrats hope that Turek’s inspiring backstory, as well as dissatisfaction with the cost of living and the agricultural trade war under Trump, could help them pick up the Hawkeye State.

Lean Republican: Texas

Texas is a recurring target for Democrats. They have poured resources into backing candidates like former Reps. Beto O’Rourke and Colin Allred, all of whom have come up short in recent Senate races. The party hopes to reverse its fortunes this year.

State Rep. James Talarico defeated Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-TX) in the party’s March primary election. Though Crockett has still not backed Talarico with the same enthusiasm that she has devoted to other candidates, the Democratic Party apparatus quickly backed Talarico.

The Republican nominating process was not nearly as clean. 

Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) had hoped to retain his seat even as Trump lashed out at the four-term senator for perceived disloyalty. Cornyn’s most formidable challenge came from state Attorney General Ken Paxton, a polarizing figure in Texas politics. Cornyn and Paxton eliminated Rep. Wesley Hunt (R-TX) and advanced to a May runoff election.

Trump provided Paxton a decisive boost when he intervened with an endorsement days before the runoff. 

“Ken Paxton has gone through a lot, in many cases, very unfairly, but he is a Fighter, and knows how to WIN,” he wrote in a May Truth Social post. “Our Country needs Fighters, and also Loyalty to the Cause of Greatness.”

Paxton pummeled Cornyn by a 28-point margin, though not without both camps spending millions of dollars that could have been reserved for the general election. The primary race between the two men cost nearly $130 million, the highest sum of this cycle.

Democrats hope to exploit Paxton’s scandal-plagued record. The attorney general was impeached by the Republican-led Texas House of Representatives in 2023 for allegedly using his office to help a political benefactor. The Texas Senate acquitted him on all charges.

Paxton’s campaign, meanwhile, has drawn attention to Talarico’s past comments on race, religion, and transgender issues.

Yet Talarico nevertheless has proven to be one of the most effective fundraisers this cycle. Talarico finished the second quarter with $21.5 million in the bank as Paxton was working to rebuild his coiffeurs from almost nothing after his primary race.

“You’ll remember, I had a runoff that lasted until May 26,” Paxton said in a Newsmax appearance this week. “On the 27th, I had zero dollars left to spend. So my opponent had three months. He didn’t have a runoff, so he raised about 30 million from mostly California. If you go look at it, most of his money comes from out of state.”

news.title: Oprah Winfrey Responds to Backlash Over Dr. Phil, Dr. Oz
news.text:
Oprah Winfrey played a pivotal role in introducing Dr. Phil and Dr. Oz to a national audience, using her daytime TV powerhouse to help transform both men into recognizable names with influence that has lasted for decades.

But the media mogul has also faced pushback for elevating two public figures whose politics and viewpoints have not always aligned with the more liberal leanings often associated with Hollywood.

Phil McGraw and Mehmet Oz each went on to headline their own television talk shows after first gaining visibility on The Oprah Winfrey Show, and both have credited Winfrey with changing the course of their careers and reshaping daytime television.

In a new interview with Emmy magazine, Winfrey, 72, defended her choice to give both men a platform, while acknowledging that their public lives have since moved in very different “paths.”

“People criticize me for Dr. Phil and Dr. Oz, because of their politics or their views. Dr. Phil, he was so practical, so down to earth, so real,” she told the publication. Winfrey recalled that McGraw would ride with her each morning as she headed to court while she was “literally sitting on trial for six weeks” during a 1998 lawsuit brought by Texas cattlemen who claimed she had damaged the beef industry’s reputation.

She said his guidance during that period left a lasting impression. “I felt that he was so instrumental in helping me. I thought, ‘Oh, you could help a lot of people. You should come on my show.’”

‘Gayle introduced me to Dr. Oz. He explained practical things like colon cancer and bowel movements. I thought he had the language for explaining medical things in a way that was helpful to me. 

‘I thought it would be helpful to many other people. And that is how they ended up on the show.

‘Everybody has their own path in life, and it has not one thing to do with me, and I don’t have one thing to do with them. At the time, the reason and intention behind me giving them their breaks was I thought they had valuable information to share that had been meaningful to me.’

A spokesman for Dr Phil told Our News Outlet, ‘Dr. Phil is eternally grateful to Oprah for the opportunity she provided him all those years ago, and for her recent kind words.

‘She’s been a brilliant mentor and a great and valued friend to Dr. Phil and his entire family, always so generous in business and spirit. Over the last almost 30 years, each of them have continued building their own very successful enterprises, some shared, while of course charting their own distinct paths in life— as one would expect. He considers her ‘one of one!”

The Daily Mail has contacted representatives for Dr Oz but have not yet heard back. 

Mehmet is now leading Trump’s Medicare and Medicaid Services while McGraw was embedded as a journalist with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Chicago and Los Angeles last year. 

In 2025, Trump asked McGraw to join the administration’s Religious Liberty Commission. 

McGraw also spoke at Trump’s Madison Square Garden rally in what he later revealed was as ‘an act of rebellion’ rather than a formal endorsement, after Vice President Kamala Harris ignored his repeated requests for an interview.

In an interview with Piers Morgan, McGraw said the speech wasn’t given to ‘endorse Donald Trump’ and would not reveal who he was voting for. During his speech, McGraw made it clear that he doesn’t ‘like or agree with everything Donald J. Trump does or says.’

‘No human is perfect. We don’t strive for perfection. We strive for excellence. But you don’t have to love everything about someone in order to love them, and the last thing he needs is some celebrity endorsement,’ he stated.

In a 2011 interview with NPR, McGraw called Winfrey ‘the gold standard’ for television and a close friend who he still worked with.

‘Well, you know, I’m in a unique situation because we are very close friends and we continue to work together. And she’s always been my mentor and helper on the Dr. Phil show, and of course that will continue. 

‘And then I’m very involved in the Oprah Winfrey Network, doing a number of projects. So I’m one of those lucky few that gets to continue to have her in my life on an ongoing basis. So I feel very fortunate about that.’ 

McGraw’s friendship with Winfrey began when he was hired on as a jury consultant after she was sued by the beef industry for disparagement in 1997 (she won the trial), according to the Texas Tribune.

Winfrey was so impressed by McGraw that she ended up featuring him on her program and eventually offering him a talk show.

‘Well you know it’s funny,’ he told DailyMailTV in 2019 of Winfrey approaching him for the show. ‘I was going by her office one day and she said “hey dummy, come in here.” She said “it’s time. We need to do it.”

Oprah informed McGraw that her show was getting a ton of mail for him and that ’80 percent of our transcripts that people order are for your shows.’

For McGraw, it was a no-brainer: ‘I said “put me in coach.” I was ready.’

Mehmet works directly with Trump as the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and recently described the president as a ‘vessel’ of vigor as he addressed his frequent medical evaluations. 

‘If you look at these records, they’re spectacular,’ Oz started.

‘You know, his cholesterol, his blood pressure – all the numbers are in excellent parameters. His ability – and I work with him frequently, many of you get to see him almost every day – that amount of energy and that amount of mental acuity does not exist in a vacuum,’ he continued. 

Winfrey met Mehmet in 2003 when Oz and his wife Lisa created a medical series called Second Opinion with Dr Oz for the Discovery Channel.

‘My friend Gayle was so intrigued by him that she encouraged me to be his first guest,’ Winfrey said in 2011, in an introduction to her interview with him for her magazine.

‘Lucky for me, Gayle isn’t just persuasive—she’s perceptive. The day of the taping, I immediately recognized what she’d sensed: a cardiac surgeon who cared as much about transforming people’s lives as he did about fixing their hearts.’

Winfrey invited Oz onto her show in 2004, and he went on to appear more than 60 times.

‘Over the years, he educated us, gave us helpful advice, and saved countless lives—from heart attack victims who, thanks to him, recognized their symptoms in time…to a cancer patient who, mindful of his warnings about medical mistakes, realized that she still had the tumor her surgeon was supposed to have removed,’ she continued.

‘He’s the reason I started wearing lower heels (my bunions are eternally grateful), and he taught me everything I know about the omentum.’

In the magazine interview, she asked him: ‘Do you have any flaws?’

The Dr Oz Show aired from 2009 to 2022.

news.title: Steve Hilton’s Chances of Beating Becerra to Flip California for GOP—Poll
news.text: Democrat Xavier Becerra held an 18-point lead over Republican Steve Hilton in a new poll of the California governor's race released on Thursday. Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom cannot run for a third term and Republicans face an uphill battle in the state, known as one of the most Democratic in the country. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won California by 20 points in the 2024 presidential race, a smaller margin than President Joe Biden’s 29-point victory four years earlier. Becerra and Hilton emerged victorious from a contentious jungle primary in June and will face off in the November general election. Whoever wins will become the leader of the nation’s most populous state that under Newsom’s leadership has led opposition against President Donald Trump’s administration. Becerra served as the secretary of Health and Human Services during the Biden administration and previously served as California’s attorney general and a member of Congress. Hilton is a conservative political commentator who served as an adviser to David Cameron, a former prime minister of the United Kingdom. Becerra spokesperson Jonathan Underland responded to the poll, which was conducted by the University of California Berkeley Institute of Government Studies, in a statement to Newsweek. “Today's poll is further confirmation that California voters support Secretary Becerra's focus on lowering the cost of living for California's working families and standing up against the hateful and disastrous policies pushed by Trump and his endorsed candidate, Steve Hilton,” Underland said. Newsweek reached out to a spokesperson for Hilton via email for comment. Becerra Leads Hilton in New California Poll The new poll, sponsored by The Los Angeles Times, showed that 55 percent of Californians plan to cast their ballot for Becerra, while 37 percent are supporting Hilton. An additional 8 percent were still undecided. Becerra received the backing of 88 percent of Democrats, while 91 percent of Republicans said they would vote for Hilton. Among independents or those registered with other parties, 58 percent said they would vote for Becerra to 30 percent for Hilton, according to the poll. The poll surveyed 2,310 likely voters August 3-9 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. The previous Berkeley IGS poll survey of registered voters showed Becerra’s support at 52 percent to Hilton's 31 percent, with 17 percent undecided. It surveyed 8,578 registered voters May 19-24, with a sampling error of plus or minus 2 percentage points. What Other Polls Show Other recent polls also show Becerra with a wide lead. A Public Policy Institute of California survey, which surveyed 1,003 likely voters June 29-July 6, showed Becerra up 25 points, 61 percent to 36 percent. Meanwhile, a Kreate Strategies poll, which surveyed 900 likely voters June 13-17, also showed Becerra leading by 25 points, 58 percent to 33 percent. Prediction markets also favor Becerra. As of Thursday, Becerra had a 95.5 percent chance of winning on Kalshi and a 93 percent chance on Polymarket. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. As of December 30, 2025, Democrats had a significant advantage in party registration in California. According to the secretary of state’s office, there were 10,381,340 registered Democrats and 5,804,699 registered Republicans. An additional 5,231,189 did not have a party preference, while 1,674,870 were registered with other parties. When Did California Last Elect a Republican Governor? Democrats have won recent elections in California, but the governorship was once viewed as more competitive. Arnold Schwarzenegger was the last Republican to win a gubernatorial election in California, with a successful reelection bid in 2006. Four years later, the governorship flipped back to Democrats under Jerry Brown and has held steady ever since. Newsom won in 2018 with nearly 62 percent of the vote and was reelected in 2022 with more than 59 percent. California remains one of the most solidly Democratic states in the nation, though it shifted rightward in 2024 as Trump made inroads with Latino voters. Still, Democrats win overwhelmingly in cities like Los Angeles, San Diego, San Francisco and other areas in the state, keeping it solidly in their hands in the latest cycles. Democrats believe the state will remain in their hands in November as Trump’s approval rating slips nationally, but Republicans believe California voters are ready for change amid concerns around homelessness and the high cost of living. Hilton previously told Newsweek that he believes 2026 could be the year California flips because of the “complete disaster” of homelessness in the state and poor education scores. “I think it's just obvious that these 16 years of Democrat progressive governance have been an unmitigated disaster, and a very expensive one, because we pay the highest taxes for these terrible results,” he said in May. “When you add all that up, I think the case for change is overwhelming." What Happens Next Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball don’t view the race as competitive, with both classifying it as safe or solid for Democrats. Polls will continue to be closely watched to gauge the mood of the electorate in California ahead of the November midterms. Hilton has challenged Becerra to a series of debates in the coming months, but it’s not clear when they will occur. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: Republicans are hoping to make California competitive in this year's midterms, but a new poll gave Becerra a double-digit lead.

news.title: President AOC? Keep dreaming
news.text:
And it could happen.

This possibility, of course, isn’t because AOC has the best ideas or brains for the country. Not even close. It’s because there are enough younger voters who believe the system is failing them and the country is broken. Blow the whole thing up, they say. And they have zero concern about the consequences.

What are those consequences? Here’s what Democratic Socialists of America intend to do if given power: 

Abolish the Senate.

Abolish the presidency. 

Abolish the Electoral College. 

Abolish the Supreme Court in its current form and expand it to the point that it looks like the New York Yankees roster. 

Add D.C. and Puerto Rico as U.S. states, thereby effectively giving the Democrats four Senate seats and permanent power in the upper chamber.

Abolish prisons. 

Abolish ICE. 

Defund the police. 

Seize major private corporations and have the government run them instead. 

Implement a 32-hour workweek. 

Cancel all student debt. 

Implement nationwide rent control. 

Provide free education from Pre-K through college. 

Allow anyone in the country illegally to vote. 

And grant all illegals permanent citizenship status. 

It’s amusing on some level and disturbing on another that establishment Democrats all got the memo to talk about how the socialist, arguably communist, takeover of the party is all part of a “big tent.”

As Bill Maher recently remarked, you know who else houses big tents? Clowns.

Take DSA co-chair Megan Romer as an example. She sat down for what was supposed to be a comfy interview with David Remnick of The New Yorker. But when Remnick actually did Journalism 101 and asked for specifics around Romer’s declaration around “taxing the hell out of millionaires,” she exposed herself as a clueless clown with no grasp of what it would look like to taxpayers.

“I think most billionaires got their wealth because they exploited the working class in some very significant way usually,” Romer told Remnick. “Are we exploiting people is the bigger question, as opposed to some sort of arbitrary red line of, ‘you can have this much money or not have that much money’? But we do believe in taxing the hell out of millionaires, yeah, absolutely.”

Remnick rightly followed up by asking Romer to clarify what kind of number she was talking about from a taxation perspective. And here was her response.

“Yeah, you know, again, I don’t have, like, a solid number,” Romer replied.

“But shouldn’t you? If you’re the co-chair of the DSA, shouldn’t you be more specific than ‘taxing the hell’ out of something?” he retorted. 

“Yeah, we need to look at what we need to pay for in the interim, what sort of tax base we need for that to happen, and build from there,” Romer said.

Another problem for the Democrat Party is that establishment officials are welcoming these clowns into that big tent. Guess what happens next: The clowns will destroy the tent and take down every establishment Democrat with them. The “E” word is a dirty one in politics today, as in “establishment.” Democrats are realizing that through the primary process, they’re going to become another “E” word: extinct.

Currently, the Democratic National Committee is already essentially extinct, at least financially. According to the FEC, the committee carries an $18.5 million debt. Its cash on hand is just $16.5 million. In contrast, the RNC has $128.5 million in cash on hand with zero debt. DNC Chairman Ken Martin, a Tim Walz protege, is barely holding on to a job that no sane member of the party wishes to inherit. 

Meanwhile, the DSA has $5.2 million on hand with zero debt.

Add it all up, and it’s hard to imagine an establishment Democrat emerging from the pack in 2028 as the party nominee. Gavin Newsom was once seen as the favorite to represent the party, but in the end, will the DSA allow for an inauthentic establishment white guy with a horrific record as governor to represent them? Will the DSA back another patently inauthentic candidate in Kamala Harris? How about Pete Buttigieg? JB Pritzker? Jon Ossoff? Mark Kelly?

As it stands now, AOC is the best candidate in this current environment to win the hearts and minds of the DSA. And she’s already moderating her radical positions.

In her friendly conversation with ABC’s Jonathan Karl on Sunday, she was asked about Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong’s past comments on defunding the police and abolishing prisons.

“I have a local city councilman that has this saying, ‘Woke 1 was crazy,'” Ocasio-Cortez told Karl, who predictably laughed along. “And I think that what’s important is that we have to assess what a candidate is saying now.”

Well, if Woke 1 was crazy, that makes AOC herself crazy.

Here is how AOC responded to a question about defunding the police in June 2020: “When a teenager or preteen does something harmful in a suburb, white communities bend over backwards to find alternatives to incarceration for their loved ones to ‘protect their future,’ like community service or rehab or restorative measures. Why don’t we treat black and brown people the same way? Why doesn’t the criminal system care about black teens’ futures the way they care for white teens’ futures?”

That sounds very Woke 1, doesn’t it? But AOC may be running to replace Chuck Schumer as a New York senator or may have her eyes on the presidency. So we’re just supposed to pretend she never said what she said just a few short years ago. And for his part, Karl didn’t bother to challenge her on any of this.

So will AOC run for president? The bet here is that she would have an excellent chance to be the nominee if the DSA continues to engulf the party. But does she have the temperament? Can she work with moderates in her own party, let alone Republicans, on a hopelessly split Capitol Hill? Because we all saw what happened in Munich earlier this year when she was asked what her response would be as president if China invaded Taiwan, and it wasn’t pretty.

“Um, you know, I think that this is such a, you know, I think that this is, this is of course a very long standing policy of the United States,” she mumbled over an awkward 20 seconds when struggling to offer a coherent response. After some rare mockery, even from legacy media, she ran to the New York Times to defend herself.

If this is how she handled her disastrous performance in Munich, how would she hold up during a two-year campaign for president? What would a debate against JD Vance or Marco Rubio look like? 

In her seven years as a lawmaker, AOC, especially for someone who is arguably the most recognizable in Congress, has not accomplished anything of substance. A nonpartisan study by the University of Virginia and Vanderbilt University ranked her 230th out of 240 members of Congress in terms of effectiveness. And among the 19 Democratic congressional members in New York State, AOC ranked last in effectiveness, according to the same study.

All sizzle, no steak. All foam, no beer. 

President Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez? It’s a dream for the DSA and many in legacy media. Once in a blue moon, dreams can come true. That won’t be the case here.

news.title: Not Winning? Just Change the Rules
news.text:
What binds the new Democratic Party to the new Democratic Socialists is a set of shared issues and values. That is, the radicalism of the Democrats in the age of Trump Derangement Syndrome — lawfare, de-balloting, the Mar-a-Lago raid, and calls to destroy the Electoral College, the nine-justice Supreme Court, and the filibuster — helped give birth to the socialists.

But the overriding commonality among those on the new Left is that if they do not get their way, they blame the "system." Then they seek to change the rules, no matter how hallowed those laws and conventions may have been or how much they themselves benefited from them in the past.

When the Left lost the White House, Congress, and, for the most part, the Supreme Court, it began clamoring to change the system. For left-wing Democrats, that angst also translated into calls to bring in two new blue states, weaponize the FBI and DOJ, ally with social media to suppress the news, and spy on congressional representatives. All the socialists and communists did was up the ante in destroying norms by calling for the end of the presidency, the Senate, the border, the police, and the Pentagon.

By 2021, it was time to destroy the southern border and welcome in some 10 million illegal immigrants — without audits, English proficiency, health checks, or the ability to support themselves.

Had Kamala Harris been elected in 2024, we would have had another four years and another five million illegal aliens. And perhaps America would have gone from 50 million foreign-born residents to 60 million, or about 18 percent of the population.

In this regard, the Left sees California as our most liberal — and most ideal — state and perhaps concludes that the reason is that 28 percent of its resident population is now foreign-born, with the majority arriving with vast needs for health, education, housing, and food subsidies.

Today, 50 percent of all births in California are paid for by Medi-Cal, which serves 40 percent of the population. When second-generation immigrants are added to the foreign-born population, the two groups together comprise roughly 45 percent of California's current population. This demographic transformation is one of the most profound in American history and came at a time when traditional civic education stressing assimilation, acculturation, integration, and knowledge of American traditions, history, and values was nearly nonexistent in California public schools.

So one way of achieving radical change was to alter the demography and welcome as many immigrants as possible who, in the first or second generation, might follow the examples of Reps. Rashida Tlaib, Ilhan Omar, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, or Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

They represent an entirely new sort of immigrant who arrives — or is born to immigrant parents — with both complaints against and dependence on their host country. They can see only the sins of America, never the catastrophes of their homeland that drove them or their parents here. This strange demand to change the rules whenever they do not bode well for angry and aggrieved parties permeates every possible manifestation of the Left, but is especially egregious when demanded by immigrants who came originally as uninvited guests but almost immediately damned their magnanimous host.

It is strange for so many new immigrants to act on an elemental desire to reach America — only on arrival to profess that it is full of toxic, sinful people, living and dead. Yet the damned hosts have inexplicably welcomed total strangers like themselves, and have allowed them to share in the freedom, security, and prosperity created by the dead whom the newcomers nonetheless endlessly slander and smear.

If particular minorities statistically did not do as well on the SAT as Asians and whites did on average, the solution was certainly not SAT tutorials in the inner city or K-12 SAT outreach, demands for tougher classes in grammar, math, and analytics, or a return to the melting pot rather than the current salad-bowl tribalist model.

Instead, after the George Floyd riots, the call went out to abolish the SAT entirely — as if there had never been a purpose behind its creation. In fact, merit-based SAT exams were designed in the 1920s and 1930s to allow anyone, regardless of race, gender, region, or class, to enter college through meritorious performance on the tests — and, in particular, to overcome old-boy insider preferences and regional and ethnic prejudices.

Yet when the SAT was mostly abolished for four or five years, higher education thought it had solved the problem of minority underrepresentation.

In fact, its racialist war on standards only magnified its dilemmas. The SAT had once informed admissions officers not only about applicants' qualifications but also whether admitted students could do the work once enrolled.

But soon liberal professors learned that many of the newly admitted cohorts lacked the K-12 training necessary to do customary university coursework. Yet if professors maintained their regular courses, requirements, and grading, they might soon be labeled racists once particular minorities were shown to do less well than Asians and whites.

So universities inflated grades. They introduced new remedial and gut courses. And they reduced the required coursework. But again, racialism is never a solution to problems. Instead, it is a catalyst that fuels them — as we have seen with the new notion that plagiarism is not an actionable offense when the culprit can plead victim status, whether a former president of Harvard or a current professor at Cambridge. But there are ancient laws and norms that insist intellectual theft is a crime and should be punished, not rewarded or ignored.

Soon employers noticed that the reading, writing, and analytical skills of graduates from prestigious schools were proving dismal. Alumni complained both that the reputations of their almae matres were in decline and resting on the fumes of the past and that their own children, who had prepared diligently to ensure suitably competitive grades and SAT scores for admission, were being rejected solely on the basis of their race.

The Left likewise pushed for lower physical standards for the military's ground-combat brigades so that women, on average far less strong than their male counterparts, could join elite units. Again, the same ignorance and arrogance were evident. Physical standards were based on a century of combat experience in which morale, group discipline, and unit success rested on ensuring that all soldiers achieved a common level of physical strength and endurance.

This neo-Marxist-driven demand to mandate equality — albeit now substituting racial and gender consciousness for class consciousness — requires the destruction of established traditions, laws, and norms. The radical Left's key agendas — defunding the police, destroying the border, granting mass amnesties to illegal aliens, subsidizing wind and solar energy while waging a war on fossil fuels, and expanding racial essentialism in hiring and admissions — have never won more than 30 to 40 percent support among the general public. Yet the solution was not to ask why, and then to reflect, reboot, and recalibrate in order to discover how the Left had lost public support.

Instead, the solution was to alter or destroy the system that had denied them power.

So communists, socialists, and radical Democrats prefer moving the goalposts. When equality of opportunity was largely achieved, next they demanded a mandated equality of outcome.

With the ascendancy of a large, affluent middle class, the Left, in its eternal search for a victimized class, pivoted and replaced class oppression with racial victimization.

And when there were not yet enough victimized minorities to guarantee a majority constituency of the aggrieved, the Left redefined the victimized to include anyone who was not a white heterosexual male, regardless of income and privilege.

And when the people finally tired of the leftists' totalitarian social engineering, the Left sought to change the system by radically altering the way Americans vote, the manner in which government is formed and functions, and, finally, the very demography of America.

The common denominator? Human nature revolts at forced statism, coercive redistribution, and government-mandated equality of results. It instead yearns for liberty and freedom.

No matter how much deception, camouflage, or brainwashing is employed, statism, socialism, and communism can never sustain public support. Throughout history, the Left has therefore begun by changing the rules and altering the demography — if not initially through changes to election rules, bureaucratic fiat, and biased court orders, then eventually through sheer violence.

news.title: What is Gen Z’s dark and nonsensical humor trying to say?
news.text:
After Luigi Mangione was arrested in December 2024 in connection with the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, the internet did what it often does: It turned something serious into a joke.

Although Mangione has pleaded not guilty to second-degree murder in New York and to federal stalking charges, viral memes at the time romanticised him as a popular – and incredibly attractive – man of the people who made corporate elites within the American health insurance industry afraid.

Some of these memes adhered to conventional forms of political satire. One, for example, quoted a speech from the movie A Bug’s Life in which a villainous grasshopper argues for the need to punish the movie’s ant protagonist to keep the other ants in line. In this meme, the political point was clear: Elites preserve power by making examples of insignificant ants who dare to challenge them.

The point was less clear with other memes, including celebrations of Mangione’s fashion-forward shackled ankles in court and mock Burger King advertisements referencing the fact that a McDonald’s employee had been the one to call law enforcement on him: “Burger King: We won’t turn you in to the Feds.” Rather than being ironic, they are unserious.

Nonetheless, memes like those received serious reactions from social commentators and political pundits who interpreted them as evidence that America’s young adults are nihilistic and morally indifferent.

As an experimental psychologist who studies moral judgments about real-world controversies, I have examined these attitudes toward Mangione and the humor surrounding him online.

I believe these reactions are better understood not as a rejection of value but as a refusal to participate in conversations that feel selective and disconnected from young people’s broader economic and political frustrations. In my assessment, Gen Z’s dark and nonsensical humor does not show a lack of moral values, but it’s instead the product of its desire to engage in more authentic conversations about what they believe.

Alienation, not indifference

Research shows deep levels of alienation among Gen Z, or young people born between 1997 and 2012. Having grown up with smartphones and social media, this generation has come of age in an increasingly online world. Despite the internet’s capacity for instantaneous interaction, followers have proved a poor replacement for friends.

Gen Z is among the most socially isolated and psychologically distressed generations on record. Compared with prior generations, fewer friendships and romantic relationships have left many young adults craving connection and solidarity. This alienation is also evident in their skepticism toward institutions and traditional narratives about values.

Many are pessimistic about achieving the American Dream and question the value of higher education. What was once considered the optimal vehicle for living a better life is instead viewed as a barrier.

If the American Dream feels out of reach, and college seems like an expensive obstacle, calls to take them seriously may feel inauthentic, alienating and absurd.

When seriousness gets suspended

Discussions about values require some seriousness if they are to resonate with their audience.

If, for example, a commencement speaker praising the value of artificial intelligence is met with jeers from graduates – as former Google CEO Eric Schmidt was in May 2026 – the speaker’s message is immediately rendered inert.

These students’ jeers fell short of offering an argument against the speaker’s claims; instead, they created an atmosphere that prevented those claims from receiving consideration. For graduates pessimistic about AI’s implications for the labor market, claims professing its value feel inauthentic.

Together, their jeers not only provided an escape from what felt like an alienating and inauthentic message about the value of AI, but they also created a sense of solidarity through a shared suspension of seriousness.

Humor offers an escape

Far from being unique to Mangione, this suspension of seriousness recurs throughout online meme culture.

The OceanGate implosion prompted similar memes, including one depicting a pod of orcas with the caption “The water is safe, send more billionaires.”

Even Charlie Kirk’s assassination became material. In a trend known as “Kirkification,” users superimposed his face onto images ranging from the Mona Lisa to women in bikinis, transforming a grim event into a shared absurdity.

In my assessment, Gen Z’s creation and circulation of memes offers an escape from otherwise serious conversations – for example, conversations about the value of the UnitedHealthcare CEO’s life. This may be especially true when demands to condemn Mangione appear to ignore inequities within an American health insurance system perceived as corrupt and unjust.

Although commentators often dismiss Gen Z’s humor as nonsensical or nihilistic meme slop, scholarship suggests that it acts as a collaborative coping mechanism, driven by a desire for authenticity.

Memes about Mangione, or even campus lookalike contests centered on him, fall short of offering a precise moral argument in favor of largely suspending seriousness.

This style of humor can be seen in Mangione’s alleged decision to leave a backpack containing Monopoly money in Central Park. It was seen, too, on shell casings recovered after Kirk’s killing, which included video game commands, a sexually suggestive internet saying and “if you read this you are gay lmao.”

Miscast explanations of nihilism

With the help of approximately a dozen undergraduate students, I examined the psychological and situational factors associated with Gen Z’s reactions to Mangione and other events – like Kirk’s assassination and the Kamala Harris is “Brat” phenomenon during the 2024 presidential election – in two studies currently under review.

Our findings indicate that favorable attitudes toward Mangione were associated not only with superficial factors, such as his perceived attractiveness, but also with higher levels of political cynicism.

Perceived systemic bias in the American justice system, for example, was addressed in a meme depicting Mangione walking into court with the text “You can kill dozens of kids and get a lesser sentence because their lives don’t matter as much as a CEO’s.” Federal prosecutors were seeking the death penalty against Mangione for a charge a judge dismissed in January 2026.

Casting Gen Z’s reactions as nihilistic obscures the values and institutional distrust connected to them and fails to appreciate their egalitarian and pragmatic ideals. Dismissing them may deepen the alienation that allowed the death of a father of two to become a joke.

Why simple moral messages alienate

Although political commentators disagree about how to interpret the response to Mangione, many accept a seemingly basic principle: Killing should never be justified.

Yet decades of research on moral judgment shows that people do not apply that principle consistently. Instead, in certain situations, like in the famous “trolley problem,” people frequently judge killing to be morally permissible – especially when that killing is expected to promote the well-being of others.

Simplistic and sweeping moral injunctions not only fail to appreciate people’s actual moral attitudes, but they also eliminate the possibility of having authentic and nuanced conversations.

Those conversations need not end by endorsing Mangione as a sympathetic figure. However, an open and authentic conversation about Mangione cannot be realised in spaces that require all discussion of the event to be reduced to affirmations that, as has been advocated by some, “Murder is bad. Period.”

Such requirements can make conversations about significant moral issues – even controversial ones, like the morality of Mangione’s alleged actions – little more than demands for conformity. In this case, those boundaries risk ignoring and, thus, further alienating Gen Z.

Gen Z’s humor shows that almost anything can become a joke. I believe the danger of that is not that young people reject values, but that continued alienation may leave them laughing when seriousness is most required.

Evan Clarkson is Assistant Professor, experimental psychology, Utah Valley University.

news.title: Is D.N.C. Chair the Worst Job in Washington?
news.text:
McAuliffe was able to avoid the job that year. The reason he was so resistant, he told me recently, was that Democrats held control of the White House at the time, making the role of the Party chair largely nominal. “If you wanted to go to the bathroom, you would call the White House political director and ask permission,” McAuliffe said. “It’s just not my personality.” McAuliffe later agreed to take the job during George W. Bush’s first term. But the truth about leading the Democratic National Committee is that, no matter who holds power, the job of chair can be, to borrow McAuliffe’s word, “miserable.”
Ken Martin, the Party’s current chair, is experiencing this right now. Martin is fifty-three and brings a low-profile approach to the job. He keeps his hair in a neat side part and wears a combination of navy suits, dress shirts, and fleeces. His overwhelming quality, in his speech and demeanor, is his Minnesotan-ness; he ran the state Party in Minnesota for fourteen years. During that time, Democrats never lost a statewide race. As chair, Martin has not been a regular presence on national television attacking Donald Trump, or an ideological leader trying to shape the future of the Democratic Party. He has positioned himself instead as a man who knows how to operate the mechanics of the Party in service of winning. Martin previously served as both a vice-chair of the D.N.C. and the head of the Association of State Democratic Committees. In short, he was supposed to understand the job. Yet, eighteen months into his tenure, the difficulties of the role appear to be winning out. Few seem happy with Ken.
Martin’s woes include claims of financial mismanagement and general dysfunction. As of the end of June, the Republican National Committee had about a hundred and twenty-eight million dollars in the bank and no debt. The D.N.C., by contrast, had about sixteen million dollars in cash—and eighteen million in debt. Last year, Martin took out a loan to support the D.N.C.’s activity, then bought Kamala Harris’s e-mail list of supporters for a staggering six and a half million dollars. (The Party has also absorbed millions of dollars of debt, since late 2024, from Harris’s failed campaign.) At the same time, Martin has been funding monthly payments to every state Party, an initiative he has described as “a fifty-seven-state-and-territory strategy.” Most of the payments are equal, meaning that territories such as Guam, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands, which don’t cast electoral votes for President, are receiving the same investment as a state like Wisconsin.
Late last month, the Times reported that, amid aggravation over these decisions, Martin has become increasingly insulated and paranoid inside the Party’s headquarters, a pinkish-yellow building near Capitol Hill, in Washington, D.C., where he relocated after taking office. In mid-July, according to the Times, he threw his phone at the desk of a staffer during a “pique of frustration,” an incident that resulted in a human-resources complaint. It was the kind of leak, other Democrats reasoned, that could have come only from Martin’s own team.
Then there is the matter of the D.N.C. “autopsy” report. The document was supposed to examine why Democrats lost to Trump in 2024. Martin had commissioned it himself, and made an explicit promise to release it to the public. “Of course it will be released,” he said soon after he became chair, in 2025. Later that year, he reneged on that promise, saying the autopsy would be a “distraction” from winning key races. The following spring, he asked to appear on the podcast “Pod Save America” to defend his decision to keep the report private. The interview, an uncomfortable conversation with the host Jon Favreau, did not help his cause. A few weeks later, Martin released the autopsy. The hundred-and-ninety-two-page document appeared to be an incomplete draft, and was filled with annotations, in bright-red text, about factual errors and unsourced claims. The report’s author, a Democratic operative named Paul Rivera, who had been friends with Martin for years, recently accused him of omitting a key chapter from the autopsy, a section questioning Joe Biden’s decision to run for a second term “instead of passing the torch.” After Rivera provided the chapter to the Times, Martin disputed his account, claiming that he had never been given the missing section. Martin has since disappeared from national television and declined almost all interview requests, including one from this magazine. Instead, he took to Substack to write a three-thousand-word post defending his tenure. In it, Martin asserts that—setting aside the D.N.C.’s negative balance sheet—the Party has raised more money than during any previous Republican Administration. “There is a story being told about the Democratic National Committee that is simply wrong,” he argues.
All of this has led to a swirl of negativity around the Party—even as Democrats are positioned to perform well in the midterms this fall. The actual functions of the D.N.C. are process-oriented: they include fund-raising, overseeing the Presidential-nominating process, planning the National Convention, supporting state Parties, and, ultimately, presiding over a voting body of about four hundred and fifty D.N.C. members, each with their own interests and loyalties. I covered the D.N.C. for years. Complaints about the organization have a way of reflecting whatever problems or rifts exist within the Party. Their annual meetings, in turn, are messy, gossip-filled affairs that are liable to go haywire in some small way. Under D.N.C. rules, it takes only one member to bring a motion up for debate. This can lead to meaningful discussion, but it can also lead to petty drama. The R.N.C., on the other hand, is more controlled, with limited press access to regular meetings. Republicans haven’t made significant changes to their Presidential-primary calendar in years. Democrats have been in a near-continuous overhaul of their nominating process since they reformed the system in 2018. Some of the differences between Republicans and Democrats are merely procedural. But even those procedures seem to speak to something ineffable about the cultures of the parties. Republicans fall in line. Democrats do so only after other possibilities have been exhausted.
Even by D.N.C. standards, it has been a difficult summer. By the time I reached out last week to Donna Brazile, a longtime Party leader who twice served as interim D.N.C. chair, she told me that she was tired of talking about it. “I genuinely need a break,” she said. “I’m heading to the gym for physical therapy and don’t feel like discussing the D.N.C. today.” In more good timing, she was scheduled to give an inspirational speech to the D.N.C.’s summer interns the following day.
Howard Dean, the former Vermont governor who became chair after his 2004 Presidential campaign, told me that part of the job is learning how to tune out the complaints, something Martin has apparently not yet mastered. “I think he’s got a thin skin,” Dean said. “But he’s on the right track.”
People are quick to compare Martin’s tenure with that of Tom Perez, the only other chair to serve while Trump has been President. When Perez took over, the Party was in a dismal state. Hillary Clinton had lost the election. Progressive voters felt that the D.N.C. had tipped the scales in Clinton’s favor during a bitter primary against Bernie Sanders. The D.N.C. had just been humiliated by a hack of its e-mail system. The staff had been reduced to fewer than a hundred people. Morale at D.N.C. headquarters was nonexistent. “You can’t overestimate how bad it was,” Sam Cornale, Perez’s chief of staff at the time, told me. Perez, a former Labor Secretary, took over promising a “turnaround job.” When they arrived at Party headquarters, they couldn’t even find a key to the chair’s office. At one point, as they searched the building, Cornale recalled, they opened a drawer and found a multimillion-dollar unpaid invoice from a polling firm.
Perez had run for chair in a crowded field of candidates, which included Pete Buttigieg, a little-known mayor from South Bend, Indiana, at the time. His main opponent in the race was Keith Ellison, then a Minnesota congressman beloved by Sanders voters. The race between Perez and Ellison was treated as an extension of the Clinton-Sanders primary. After Perez won the race, he named Ellison as his deputy and embarked on a “unity tour” with Sanders. Inevitably, at almost every stop on the tour, Perez would be booed. “It will never go down as one of my favorite jobs—period, hard stop,” Perez said. “But it was an important job.”
Perez’s successor was Jaime Harrison, the former Party chairman of South Carolina. Harrison held the role during the Biden Administration—and he was, just as McAuliffe warned, an extension of the White House. He has channelled his feelings about his time as chair into an upcoming memoir. The title, he told me, is, “A Chair with No Table.”
As a D.N.C. member himself, Martin was often a thorn in the side of the chair, agitating on behalf of state Parties for more resources. Now he is on the receiving end of such complaints, living in Washington, away from his wife and family in Minnesota, and spending much of his time on the road for work. It has been an adjustment. Martin isn’t well connected among major donors, or among leadership on Capitol Hill. Both Hakeem Jeffries, the House Minority Leader, and Chuck Schumer, the Senate Minority Leader, supported Ben Wikler, Martin’s opponent in the race for the chair. And many of the staffers working around him inside D.N.C. headquarters were inherited, rather than chosen by him.
Nevertheless, Martin’s fifty-seven-state-and-territory strategy has led to recruitment, staff hires, and organizing programs across the country. According to one D.N.C. official, investments in Democratic state and territory Parties, which total a million dollars a month, have helped North Carolina and Texas assemble a full slate of Democratic candidates for the first time in recent history. In Mississippi, the money has funded the hiring of new data and communications staffers. Tennessee has a new finance director. North Dakota hired part-time organizers and a part-time data director. Missouri opened a headquarters in Jefferson City. Arizona launched a Democratic voter-registration initiative. Colorado started a rural organizing program.
This weekend, Martin will convene the members of the D.N.C. in Austin, Texas, for their annual summer meeting. There has been talk of whether someone will make a move to force him out of the role. This doesn’t seem likely, as there has thus far been no discernible movement by D.N.C. members to call for his removal. To do so would require multiple procedural steps under Robert’s Rules of Order before an actual vote is taken. Minyon Moore, a leader inside the D.N.C. who has worked alongside multiple chairs, has been encouraging Martin to stick to his plans. “You have to put on your own armor, because you will not survive this if you allow every story to change the type of work that you’re doing,” she said. It remains to be seen whether Martin’s strategies will pay off. Observers worry about his fund-raising strategy, the botched autopsy rollout, the mood in the office. Can Martin restore trust in his abilities as a leader? He seems to believe that he can. Winning elections in the midterms, several former chairs told me, would certainly help. And, if anything can be learned from the modern history of the D.N.C., it is that these complaints will likely recede, and new complaints, about this or something else, will soon emerge.
When I spoke with McAuliffe, the Democrat who perhaps liked the job the best of any recent Democratic Party chair, he told me that he, too, was headed to Austin this weekend. He had just received an invitation to deliver a speech to the D.N.C. membership—a pep talk of sorts. He agreed, rescheduling a golfing trip to Ireland with his sons to be able to attend.
“I know why I’m there—to do the big rah-rah,” he told me.
What did he plan to tell his party? “Democrats! Quit your whining!” he said. “Stop your lemon-sucking. Get in the game.” ♦
news.summary: The organization is holding its annual summer meeting, and onlookers are calling for the head of its leader, Ken Martin. Then again, the Democrats are always doing that kind of thing.

news.text:
Outside Washington

Wisconsin’s Francesca Hong may have gotten most of the Democratic gubernatorial headlines this week, but in the Southwest, two other party hopefuls are making unusual pitches to the public as well. In Texas, a central component of gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa’s message, writes the Houston Chronicle’s Jeremy Wallace, is that she’s the only thing standing between America and a near-permanent GOP majority in Congress via gerrymandering and new census counts. (Wallace breaks down the numbers.) In Arizona on Tuesday, Governor Katie Hobbs announced the running mate pick that she’s been teasing for over a week, naming former Republican Mesa Mayor John Giles to her ticket. Giles, an independent now, split with his party in 2021 over a nondiscrimination ordinance intended to protect LGBTQ+ residents and endorsed Kamala Harris for president in 2024. He is also, the Arizona Capitol Times notes, “a member of the typically conservative Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, a religious affiliation he shares with Hobbs’ opponent, Congressman Andy Biggs.” 

Is a new, underwater front opening in the data center wars? Maine Public profiles a new proposal to build a “submerged” data center in Passamaquoddy Bay. The idea was famously tested in Microsoft’s Project Natick off the coast of Scotland in a pilot program that hasn’t been active in years; Maine Public notes that “earlier this year, another submerged data center was reportedly deployed in China.” Residents of Eastport, Maine, who worry about damage to the local economy, particularly if the data center heat drives out the lobsters, are having none of it. “Speakers from across the political spectrum lambasted the idea” at a recent gathering, Maine Public reports. One of the more memorable quotes, from Eastport City Manager Brian Schuth: “I have said it’s the equivalent of an idea scrawled on a bar napkin.” Of note: Both chambers of Maine’s state legislature passed a temporary moratorium on data centers larger than 20 megawatts this past spring—a measure spearheaded by state Democrats—only for Democratic Governor Janet Mills to veto. The measure would not have affected Passamaquoddy Bay, though, as the application by developer DeepGreen Western Passage would not meet this threshold. —Heather Souvaine Horn

The Ideas Factory

Resources for the Future publishes a new working paper from Yanjun “Penny” Liao, Hannah Druckenmiller, and Margaret A. Walls on the urgent topic of how weather extremes are affecting the federal crop insurance program, or FCIP. Unsurprisingly, they write, “farmers respond to adverse weather and yield shocks by increasing insurance participation: a 10 percent yield decline increases insured acreage by approximately 4.9 percent for corn and 3.4 percent for soybeans.” That means that “climate-driven enrollment growth alone is estimated to raise program costs by 4–9 percent for corn and soybeans by midcentury.” On the bright side, they also find that “FCIP enrollment substantially mitigates the adverse effects of extreme heat on rural labor markets and generates positive spillovers to nontradable sectors, such as retail, hospitality, and health care.”

news.title: Oprah Winfrey addresses criticism for making two pro-Trump TV personalities famous
news.text:
Oprah Winfrey has addressed her part in platforming the careers of pro-Trump doctors Dr. Phil McGraw and Dr. Mehmet Oz on her titular talk show.

Winfrey’s The Oprah Winfrey Show show aired from 1986-2011. She introduced McGraw — who is no longer a licensed psychologist after letting his license lapse two decades ago — as a weekly expert and relationship strategist in 1998. Oz, who holds medical and business degrees from the University of Pennsylvania, began appearing on the program as a medical expert in 2004.

Both TV doctors have since become allies of President Donald Trump and his MAGA movement. 

McGraw, AKA Dr. Phil, serves on Trump’s Religious Liberty Commission and promotes MAGA initiatives through his conservative cable network Merit Street Media and accompanied ICE agents to a raid in Chicago with his TV network in June 2025 for a “first-hand look at the target operations.”

Oz was appointed to lead the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in 2025, and has consistently supported Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again agenda.

In a new interview with Emmy Magazine, Winfrey admitted that she faces criticism for having platformed the pair because of their current political views, but was defensive about why she chose them to join her show in the first place.

“Everybody has their own path in life, and it has not one thing to do with me, and I don’t have one thing to do with them,” she said.

“At the time, the reason and intention behind me giving them their breaks was I thought they had valuable information to share that had been meaningful to me,” she continued.

Winfrey praised McGraw for supporting her during a 1997 lawsuit, where she was sued by a group of Texas cattlemen for defaming the beef industry. She won the case in February 1998.

“He was so practical, so down to earth, so real,” she said of McGraw. “He would ride in the car with me every morning on the way to trial, where I’m literally sitting on trial for six weeks.”

Winfrey said her best friend Gayle King introduced her to Oz.

“He explained practical things like colon cancer and bowel movements,” Winfrey said. “I thought he had the language for explaining medical things in a way that was helpful to me. I thought it would be helpful to many other people. And that is how they ended up on the show.”

While Winfrey and Trump were on friendly terms before he became president, she publicly endorsed Kamala Harris during the 2024 election and delivered a speech at the Democratic National Convention.

Both McGraw and Oz’s medical expertise has been scrutinized by health professionals over the years. 

At the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, McGraw faced backlash for suggesting social distancing was unnecessary and sharing inaccurate statistics about non-contagious causes of death.

“The fact of the matter is we have people dying, 45,000 people a year die from automobile accidents, 480,000 from cigarettes, 360,000 a year from swimming pools, but we don’t shut the country down for that,” McGraw said on Laura Ingraham’s The Ingraham Angle. 

McGraw has previously said he sends a letter to Winfrey each year to express his gratitude for their friendship and how it changed his life.

“Oprah and I met in the late ‘90s when she was on trial, and I was on the trial team, then I started doing the show, and started doing the show a lot,” he said on The Kelly Clarkson Show in 2022. “And then we launched the [Dr. Phil] show, and it really changed my life a lot.”

“I had a great life when I met her, and I’ve got a great life now, but she changed a lot of things,” he said.
news.summary: TV personalities are now closely aligned with the president’s MAGA movement

news.title: The Dems' Great White Hope Just Got Humiliated in Michigan
news.text:
Pity poor Gavin Newsom, whose national ambitions — thankfully for those of us who don't live in California — appear permanently stymied by his conspicuous corruption and incompetence. The latest evidence comes from Michigan, where the would-be Democrat presidential contender was just humiliated in the state's deepest indigo of blue enclaves. 

Calling it Newsom's "swing (and miss) state tour," Politico reported on Wednesday that his "buzzy X posts and vertical videos" from Michigan "this week suggest a slam dunk trip to an early nominating state."

But even though Newsom's social media feed racked up "a million views of a 65-hour tour," Politico noted that "the posts may also be the latest sign that social media is not real life."

Translation: It was a trip notable mostly for bad execution and embarrassing turnout. 

Rep. Debbie Dingell, "the Downriver doyenne largely responsible for nearly securing Michigan’s status as the fifth 2028 nominating state," told the magazine, "I didn’t hear from the governor. I didn’t expect to: I’m a car girl." That's likely in reference to Newsom's 2035 mandate banning new ICE vehicle sales in California.

Newsom snubbed Virgie Rollins, whom Politico described as "the influential chair for the DNC’s Black Caucus."

There's more:

Some Michigander politicos pointed out that Newsom canceled a fundraiser with state AG nominee Eli Savit that included the controversial host Kelly Neumann, according to an invite obtained by POLITICO and circulated to some Democrats who didn’t realize the event was canceled when Newsom’s team was made aware of Neumann’s background.Newsom initially planned two competing fundraisers in Ann Arbor on Sunday, one for Savit and one for the state House Democrats. When the latter found out about the Savit fundraiser they pulled out, citing a small Ann Arbor donor base.

Sayin Ann Arbor has a small Democrat donor base is like saying you couldn't spot any tech bros in Palo Alto. 

“He had a lot of good meetings,” Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel told Politico, adding Newsom was a big hit at a local barbecue.

I believe this was the barbecue:

Gavin Newsom pulling a massive crowd of 17 septuagenarians in Michigan. Yeah he's DEFINITELY gonna be the nominee for President. LMAO. pic.twitter.com/GrLf3Ebc2X— Spencer Pratt (@spencerpratt) August 11, 2026

Yikes, how the mighty have fallen.

Then again, "Newsom huddled for nearly an hour with Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed," if you want to know the governor's current priorities.

Politico argued that "it’s also true that some of the hard feelings may underscore just how much Newsom is in demand," but I'm not sure I see it.

I wouldn't be too surprised if Newsom 2028 ended up following a similar path to Kamala Harris 2020. It makes me smile every time I remember that the Dems' Queen of Summer 2019 ended up dropping out of the race in December, weeks before the Iowa caucuses — her polls cratering almost as quickly as her coffers. 

It's no coincidence that they're both from California. As my partner in thoughtcrime, Stephen Kruiser, and I have discussed several times over the years, the Golden State is maybe the nation's worst breeding ground for Democrats with presidential ambitions.

Once a Dem woos the right money people — particularly Nancy Pelosi, but she's now fading — they never really have to compete. Or even learn how to compete. Taking a Democrat like Harris or Newsom out of California is like taking the Boy in the Bubble out of confinement and directly into Wuhan Institute of Virology on a particularly leaky day.

Besides, as conservative Hollywood scribe George MF Washington put it on X this morning, "The energy of his party is done with straight white men."

Maybe I'm wrong. Maybe Newsom has learned the lessons Harris never did. Maybe he really is the Democrats' Great White Hope. But I didn't see much evidence of that in Michigan.
