news.title: Trump Says Black Voters Are Flocking to GOP — New Data Suggests Otherwise
news.text: President Donald Trump said that Black and Brown voters are "flocking" to the Republican Party, but recent polling contradicts his claims, showing that his approval rating among these groups has plummeted. Trump made the claim on Sunday on his social media platform, Truth Social, writing: "Black and Brown Voters don’t want Communism or Socialism—Not surprisingly, they are flocking to the Republican Party! They remember that Abraham Lincoln was a Republican!" The underlying message is one that the president has tried to convey many times before: the Democratic Party, led by progressives like New York City’s Zohran Mamdani, has moved so far to the left that it is alienating American voters. But recent polls show that voters, instead of "flocking" to the GOP, are actually turning their back on the president and his administration amid rising inflation following the start of the Iran war—including Black and Hispanic voters. While Trump’s approval has fallen among Americans overall, the decline has been particularly severe among Black voters. His net approval rating among Black respondents is more than six times worse than his overall national rating, according to the latest Economist/YouGov survey. In response to a request for comment by Newsweek, White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said: "President Trump has done more for Black Americans than any other President in recent history. During the President’s first term, he implemented policies that resulted in record-low unemployment for Black Americans, established opportunity zones, and provided long-term funding for Historically Black Colleges and Universities. "The second Trump administration is building on those tremendous successes by making our communities safe and beautiful, stopping the flow of illegal migrants who were undermining American workers, signing the largest working-class tax cut in American history, and putting American children on a path toward generational wealth through Trump Accounts." Black and Hispanic Voters Increasingly Disapprove of Trump’s Handling of His Job While a majority voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, Black and Hispanic voters did shift right, particularly men and young people. A majority of 51 percent of Hispanic voters supported Harris in 2024, according to Cornell University data, against 46 percent who backed Trump; that was up from 65 percent who voted for Joe Biden in 2020 and 32 who supported Trump then. Trump also nearly doubled his support among Black voters between 2020 and 2024, according to Pew Research data. While 8 percent voted for him in 2020, 13 percent did so in 2024. Even so, an overwhelming majority (83 percent) voted Democratic. But whatever advancements Trump had made with these groups have started to unravel in recent months, as the president’s approval rating fell amid all voters over concerns for the U.S. economy. Trump’s net approval rating among Black voters has dropped by 25 points since May, according to polls by The Economist/YouGov. The most recent poll, conducted between August 7 and 10 among 1,589 U.S. adults, found that just 13 percent of Black respondents approve of the president’s handling of his job, against 79 percent who disapprove of it. That gives the president a net approval rating of -66 with Black voters, the lowest since his return to the White House. By comparison, 22 percent of Black voters said they approved of Trump’s job performance, while 69 percent disapproved, giving him a net approval rating of -47. Since then, Trump’s net approval among Black voters has steadily declined. In polls conducted in June and July, it was -54 and -64 respectively. Approval rates among Hispanic voters have similarly declined. In the latest poll, only 27 percent of Hispanic respondents approved of Trump’s handling of his job as president, while 66 percent disapproved, for a net approval of -39. Overall, Trump’s net approval rating among all Americans in the latest The Economist/YouGov poll was -10. Black Voters Aren’t Happy About the Economy—and Data Backs Them Up Significantly, the latest The Economist/YouGov poll shows that only 16 percent of Black voters think the American economy is currently in an "excellent" or "good" state, while 81 percent say it is doing fairly or poorly. Similarly, 17 percent of Hispanic voters think the economy is doing positively, while 78 percent believe it is doing poorly. Overall, 22 percent of Americans think the economy is doing well and 75 percent believe the opposite. For Black voters, their unhappiness about the state of the U.S. economy reflects the fact that they are now in the worst financial position they have been in a decade, according to a recent analysis of Federal Reserve data published by the Economic Policy Institute (EPI). After a year of what researchers call the "Trump economy," economic instability among Black households has gotten worse, with the latest Federal Reserve’s Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking (SHED) showing an increase in the number of Black adults worried about finding or keeping a job, and a decrease in those saying they are doing OK or living comfortably in 2025. "The latest SHED survey […] shows that the harm caused by the administration’s economic chaos has not affected all people equally," EPI researchers wrote. "Structural inequities embedded in the U.S. economy and labor market have historically left communities of color disproportionately vulnerable to economic insecurity and poverty, and the Federal Reserve’s survey shows that this trend is continuing," they added. "While the overall financial well-being of most adults held steady in 2025, the financial well-being of Black adults declined." In 2025, the share of Black adults "doing OK" or "living comfortably" declined by almost five percentage points last year to 60 percent—the lowest figure SHED has recorded since 2015. By comparison, 68 percent of Black adults thought they were doing financially well. Black adults were also more likely to experience layoffs, with the share of workers let go rising from 10 percent in 2024 to 12.7 percent in 2025. Similarly, layoffs increased sharply among Hispanic adults as well (from 8.2 percent to 9.6 percent), while among White voters they went up to 5.4 percent from 4.7 percent. Federal labor market data have also shown Black workers continue to face higher unemployment rates than White workers, a long-standing disparity that economists say leaves Black households more exposed to economic downturns. Possibly because they faced such a significant increase in layoffs, Black adults were much more likely to be concerned about finding a job or keeping one (from 46.4 percent in 2024 to 55.1 percent in 2025) than Hispanic adults (from 46.9 percent to 54.9 percent) and white adults (from 30.3 percent to 32.5 percent). Their growing employment vulnerability, combined with the impact of the ongoing affordability crisis, is making Black households more worried about how to get through the end of the month. According to EPI, the share of Black adults reporting that making ends meet was at least a minor concern for them and their families surged by about eight percentage points between 2024 and 2025. In contrast, the share of white, non-Hispanic adults who reported similar concerns declined marginally during the same period. What Does This Mean for Trump and the GOP? The recent polling and plunge in approval rating for the president do not necessarily erase the gains Trump made among Black and Hispanic voters in the 2024 presidential election. But they suggest that those gains may be under pressure as economic concerns mount, threatening the Republican Party as it approaches the upcoming midterms—and potentially, the 2028 election. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Ben Kelly and Robert Greenall
news.summary: Trump’s net approval rating has plunged to -66 among Black voters and -39 among Hispanic voters, according to latest polling.

“People in this country work so damn hard and still feel so damn broke. That’s no way to live,” he continues. “Susan Collins keeps telling us that everything’s fine, but we know it’s not. We all have eyes, paychecks, and bills. We know we’re getting screwed. You deserve better.”

The race has quickly proven competitive. A Fox News poll conducted Aug. 6 to Aug. 10 found Jackson leading Collins 48% to 46%, within the poll’s 3-point margin of error. The Cook Political Report likewise rated the contest a toss-up.

Jackson has also consolidated support from prominent Democrats since winning the nomination. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY), and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA) have backed his candidacy. Schumer and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chairwoman Kirsten Gillibrand said Jackson is “well-positioned” to defeat Collins after harnessing “grassroots energy in Maine.”

Jackson also has the backing of the Maine chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), who had previously endorsed Platner.

Republican Senate campaign arm previews messaging offensive exposing Democratic hypocrisy

news.title: Anti-Israel progressives benefit from lack of pushback in primaries - analysis
news.text:
One of the biggest lessons from Tuesday’s Democratic primaries is that when the old guard pushes back on the far left, or at least declines to get behind it, there’s still a chance of victory.

Another is that it's one thing to be anti-Israel. It's another to completely go off the deep end.

In a critical Senate primary in Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan whipped centrist Rep. Angie Craig.

Flanagan has accused Israel of “genocide” and asserted that she would have voted to cut off military aid to the Jewish state.

Meanwhile, Craig was among the fewer than half of House Democrats who voted to oppose severing defense aid, and Flanagan hit Craig on the latter’s support for Israel and previous endorsements from AIPAC, even as the pro-Israel group did not endorse her or directly contribute to her campaign this time around.

Flanagan moves on to face former national sportscaster Michele Tafoya, who easily won the Republican nomination. But even with high name recognition, Tafoya, who is making her entry into politics, faces an uphill climb given Minnesota's blue bent.

Craig’s struggles were reflected in her own district. Former state Sen. Matt Little, who ran furthest to the left and the harshest on Israel, handily defeated a pair of centrists for the Democratic nomination for that House seat.

Among those moderates was state Sen. Matt Klein, an advocate for Israel.

Little is favored to win against Republican nominee Eric Pratt, a state senator, in a relatively moderate district that Kamala Harris carried by only six points in the 2024 presidential election.

AIPAC-endorsed Rep. John Larson lost his reelection bid in a Connecticut House race, falling heavily to former Hartford mayor Luke Bronin. Larson, who has struggled with health issues, will see his 14-term House career in the state’s most populous Jewish district come to an end.

Larson, like Craig, had voted against the majority of House Democrats on the Israel aid issue, and AIPAC raised some $130,000 to try to extend his term.

Bronin, meanwhile, said he’ll oppose offensive weapons for Jerusalem, while keeping Iron Dome support intact.

The exception to Tuesday’s not-good-at-all results for Israel supports was in the Wisconsin gubernatorial race, where State Assembly member Francesca Hong, aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, fell to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley in the Democratic primary.

Hong, though, didn’t just take on the establishment on Israel, but on everything, essentially running on a DSA platform, including defunding the police and even canceling Thanksgiving.

Polls showed her leading, but outcry from Democratic officials, including sitting Gov. Tony Evers, appeared to bring attention to her extreme positions, potentially saving the race for Crowley and for Democrats intent on hanging on to the governor’s seat.

Even progressive stalwarts like Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez didn’t speak out on Hong’s behalf.

It brought into stark contrast the way Michigan officials handled the Senate race there, where earlier this month, anti-Israel radical Abdul El-Sayed defeated Israel-backer Rep. Haley Stevens, in what many view as a national bellwether.

Few officials there went to bat for Haley, and even those that did were loath to criticize El-Sayed. Their prescience, or reckoning, will come in November, when El-Sayed faces former Rep. Mike Rogers, in a state where a Republican hasn’t claimed a Senate seat in 32 years.

news.title: Ex-Insider Literally Claims Donald and Melania Trump Are 'Clearly Not Living Together' Right Now
news.text: Former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci has claimed that President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump are 'clearly not living together' during his second presidency, alleging the couple have 'grown apart' since returning to the White House last year.The explosive assertion came during an appearance on the podcast, where Scaramucci suggested the presidential marriage has entered a rocky patch marked by physical separation and emotional distance.Melania Trump announced at the start of Trump's second term that she would split her time between Washington, New York City and Palm Beach, citing her son Barron's studies at New York University as the primary reason.However, reports now indicate Barron has transferred to an NYU campus in Washington, yet the first lady's whereabouts remain unclear, fuelling speculation about the state of the Trumps' relationship.Scaramucci's Claims About Donald and Melania Trump Living ArrangementsScaramucci, who served a turbulent 10-day stint as White House communications director in July 2017 before being ousted following a profanity-laced media tirade, told the podcast host, 'I think it's distant for a number of different reasons. But I think they probably have grown apart.'When pressed specifically on their marriage, he added, 'It's pretty clear that they're not living together.' He noted, however, that their separate living situations do not prevent them from appearing together in public.The former hedge fund manager, who has been highly critical of Trump since his departure and endorsed both Joe Biden in 2020 and Kamala Harris in 2024, said he has maintained a 'good rapport' with Melania despite his falling out with the president.'She was always very nice to me,' Scaramucci said. 'I always liked her, my wife liked her. She was down to earth, classy.'Scaramucci also suggested the Trump family unit that entered the White House in 2017 struggled with the intensity of Washington life.'The family unit that came into Trump 1.0 didn't like it,' he elaborated. 'They didn't like the blistering in Washington. They didn't like the 360-degree firing squad. I don't think they like the spotlight that was put on them.'Previous Reports of Tensions Between Donald and Melania TrumpThis is not the first time relationship difficulties between the president and first lady have surfaced.According to Regime Change, a book released earlier this year by reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, tensions have been apparent for years, particularly over Trump's decision to demolish the 123-year-old White House East Wing to build a 90,000-square-foot ballroom expected to cost up to $1 billion (£740 million).'Mrs. Trump, who preferred a quiet environment with minimal disturbances and objected to living in a construction zone, had repeatedly expressed concern about the size and location of the ballroom,' Haberman and Swan wrote.'For several weeks in early 2025, White House aides had tried accommodating the couple's competing desires about the future of the complex.' Trump ultimately prevailed, approving the demolition despite his wife's objections.The book also reveals the couple maintain separate bedrooms, with Melania occupying the master bedroom and Trump taking over the adjacent space labelled as the second-floor 'living room.'This arrangement reportedly sparked a bizarre decor war, with Trump allegedly moving items from Melania's selected spaces into his own bedroom when she was not around.'Once, when staff gently reminded the president that he was taking things from the Center Hall his wife had personally selected, he made clear he didn't care,' the authors wrote. news.text:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Inflation eased slightly last month. Consumer prices in July were 3.4% higher than they were a year ago, according to a new report from the Labor Department. It's a smaller annual increase than in May or June. Rent and airfare prices rose while gasoline and grocery prices fell. In particular, lettuce prices plunged 16% after a deadly Cyclospora illness outbreak led to a recall of iceberg lettuce from Mexico. Retailers responded with deep discounts on various lettuce products in an attempt to win back anxious shoppers.

🎧 Produce prices often fluctuate depending on growing conditions and other factors, and lettuce prices are expected to rebound once the food scare passes, NPR's Scott Horsley tells Up First. The lower prices contributed to about 0.1% decline in grocery costs last month, but overall grocery prices are still up about 2.7% over the past year. This week's cooler inflation report may lead the Federal Reserve to monitor whether inflation will continue to moderate rather than raise interest rates, Horsley says.

Rescue teams in Colombia are urgently searching for survivors of Monday's 7.4 magnitude earthquake, which killed more than 260 people. Nearly 500 people remain missing, and the chances of finding survivors decrease each day.

🎧 It's still possible for search and rescue teams to find survivors amid the rubble at this point in their efforts, says reporter John Otis. Otis is in Cali, one of the hardest-hit areas by the quake. It's been three days since the deadly quake, and he spoke with rescue workers from other disasters who have successfully pulled people from collapsed buildings after six days. The warm weather in Cali can help trapped individuals survive, he says. Even so, Colombian officials know that they are racing against the clock. Cali's mayor has called for residents to avoid the disaster zone to give rescue teams room to work and the silence their listening devices need to detect signs of life.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement plans to equip its officers with high-tech gloves that deliver electric shocks to people they are trying to detain, according to plans posted by the Department of Homeland Security this week. The devices, known as the G.L.O.V.E., or Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, could cost DHS as much as $20 million. It delivers an electric shock upon contact with the skin when the wrist button is activated. Demonstrations indicate that the gloves inflict pain. Naureen Shah, ACLU's director of policy and government affairs for immigration, raised concerns about whether ICE officers are adequately trained to handle such devices, especially with the agency's effort to rapidly hire more than 12,000 officers within a year.

It's unclear if the organization employs immigration lawyers, though its website says it offers "legal support to help prosecute offenders."

Three tiny, but tony, neighborhoods will bear the brunt: Georgetown, Kalorama and Massachusetts Avenue Heights.

Nonsense: Billionaire Mike Bloomberg blew through hundreds of millions of dollars of his own money seeking the Democratic presidential nomination in 2020 — and won support only from American Samoa.

 As Cato economists Adam Michel and Chris Edwards warn, taxing wealth takes capital out of these companies, limiting worker productivity gains and the growth in future wages. Ouch!

Wake up, America: You, too, are in the “Tax the Rich” crosshairs.

news.title: With U.S. midterm elections looming, Democrats are clashing over how to win
news.text:
As the U.S. heads toward the midterm elections, a gruelling primary season has further entrenched a rift between the insurgent progressive and centrist wings of the Democratic Party. 

At stake is control of Congress this November and, beyond that, the presidency in 2028. 

The centrists argue candidates touting moderate and pragmatic policies is the path to flipping seats from Republican control. While progressives say more uninspiring, establishment candidates will not galvanize a coalition of young people, the working class and diverse voters that could propel the party to victory. 

"I don't even know how I could go about being sure which group has the most appeal," said Hans Noel, an associate professor of Government at Georgetown University and co-director of the Georgetown Democracy Initiative.

He says that while progressive candidates may alienate some voters who otherwise might have voted Democrat, they will also bring new voters to the party, including those who may not have voted at all. 

There are also intangible characteristics, like personal likeability, said Noel: "How do you add that all up and make a strong prediction? It's hard." 

Primary wins and losses 

The primary season — where Democratic voters choose their candidates for upcoming general elections against Republicans — has given both sides wins, losses and lessons.

On Tuesday, in the key battleground state of Wisconsin progressives were dealt a blow when democratic voters narrowly chose moderate David Crowley in the primary for governor over self-described Democratic Socialist Francesca Hong, who was projected to win in the polls. 

Hong's campaign was plagued in its final days by past comments she made advocating for defunding the police and abolishing ICE and also saying it was time to "cancel Thanksgiving," calling it a celebration of colonialism. During the campaign, she backed away from all these comments, saying her views had evolved. 

Hong ultimately wasn't endorsed by progressive flagbearers, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Sen. Bernie Sanders. 

Other races where moderates were able to hold progressive challengers at bay included those in Washington and Missouri. 

In the swing state of Michigan earlier this month, however, progressive Addul El-Sayed, who campaigned with Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders, eked out a victory against centrist candidate Haley Stevens despite over $60 million being spent on her behalf, largely from super PACs. 

El-Sayed, like other progressive candidates, campaigned on issues like medicare for all, getting money out of politics, taxing billionaire wealth and calling for an end to military aid for Israel. He has also been praised for his communication skills. 

In response to the U.S. President Donald Trump calling him "full of shit," El-Sayed shot back: "At least I don't let mine go all over the Oval Office." 

Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan's Democratic Senate primary in major victory for party's progressive wingMichigan's Democratic Senate primary puts spotlight on big money and pro-Israel lobby

El-Sayed's victory followed wins from progressive candidates who took on more moderate democrats in strongholds of New York and Colorado. 

Notably, in Maine, another battleground state, progressive Graham Platner delivered a win before he dropped out due to sexual assault allegations. 

Discontent among young voters 

Bhaskar Sunkara, president of left-leaning magazine The Nation and former vice chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, says El-Sayed's win and others like it are a "huge check" on the Democratic Party. 

"Voters, particularly young voters, are really discontent with the leadership of the party … and just generally feel that the Democratic Party doesn't stand for anything. It's not combative enough." 

Sunkara went on to say that El-Sayed is a better candidate than Hong with working-class voters. 

"I think there is a way in which some candidates have been tarred with stances they had in 2019, 2020. This sort of abolish the police, the discussion of whiteness or whatever else. Abdul never had that problem." 

Hong wasn't the only candidate backing off from past comments. 

New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made headlines earlier this week when asked about her past support for defunding the police. "I have a local city councilman that has this saying: 'Woke 1 was crazy,' " she said before laughing. 

Can progressives win key battleground states? 

While some in the progressive wing re-evaluate past positions that could alienate voters this election cycle, many moderate democrats continue to warn of liabilities in swing states. 

Fareed Zakaria, host of CNN's Sunday public affairs program GPS, cited Washington Post data to point out that while El-Sayed had the support of Michigan's most educated counties and college towns, his opponent did better in rural and lower-income areas. 

AnalysisWhat the Graham Platner scandal says about Democratic Party's troublesMore Americans than ever are identifying as political independents, poll shows

"The left has the passion, but the middle still has the votes needed to win in general elections," Zakaria said. 

Kate de Gruyter is the vice-president of communications at Third Way, a leading centrist democratic group that is spending $15 million between now and 2028 to discredit Democratic Socialism. 

"Their theory of the case is that they're somehow going to be able to persuade all these voters in the middle that they absolutely need to win in November to back their candidate. We've never seen that happen over the entirety of the Trump era," she said in an interview. 

De Gruyter added that El-Sayed's decision to campaign with controversial left-wing streamer Hasan Piker as one example of "a whole universe of things that Republican ad makers are salivating at."

De Gruyter went on to suggest that the reason Democrat Kamala Harris lost the presidential election in 2024 was that she was seen as too lax on issues like immigration and plagued by stances she'd taken in the past on "transgender policy." 

Democrats' autopsy of 2024 U.S. election blames Harris and 'identity politics' for lossKamala Harris says she 'might' make another presidential run in 2028

In the final weeks of the campaign. Trump's team ran an ad using a five-year old clip of Harris saying that "every transgender inmate in the prison system would have access" to taxpayer-funded gender transitions.

"The idea that we should move further left makes no sense at all," she said. 

The interesting thing is that while that can all be true, there are also plenty of arguments that suggest the opposite, according to Noel, the Georgetown associate professor. 

"And it can also be true that Harris actually lost because she was too tied to the establishment and Biden. And too close to Israel … progressives called her a cop. Either of those differences could have been enough because it was a fairly close race." 

Either way, Democrats are riding favourable waves into the midterms. 

Trump's polling is low. He has entered into an unpopular war in Iran. And all of this should help the Democrats, whether they're progressives or moderates in the mid-terms, said Noel, adding that if the Democrats don't do as well as expected there will be a lot of "what happened?"

"If all the progressive candidates lose and the centrist candidates win, well, that's going to be an easier story."

Centrists argue moderate and pragmatic policies are key to flipping seats, while progressives say more inspiring candidates are needed to galvanize young people, the working class and diverse voters.

"I don't even know how I could go about being sure which group has the most appeal," said Hans Noel, an associate professor of Government at Georgetown University and co-director of the Georgetown Democracy Initiative.

He says that while progressive candidates may alienate some voters who otherwise might have voted Democrat, they will also bring new voters to the party, including those who may not have voted at all. 

There are also intangible characteristics, like personal likeability, said Noel: "How do you add that all up and make a strong prediction? It's hard." 

Primary wins and losses 

The primary season — where Democratic voters choose their candidates for upcoming general elections against Republicans — has given both sides wins, losses and lessons.

On Tuesday, in the key battleground state of Wisconsin progressives were dealt a blow when democratic voters narrowly chose moderate David Crowley in the primary for governor over self-described Democratic Socialist Francesca Hong, who was projected to win in the polls. 

Hong's campaign was plagued in its final days by past comments she made advocating for defunding the police and abolishing ICE and also saying it was time to "cancel Thanksgiving," calling it a celebration of colonialism. During the campaign, she backed away from all these comments, saying her views had evolved. 

Hong ultimately wasn't endorsed by progressive flagbearers, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Sen. Bernie Sanders. 

Other races where moderates were able to hold progressive challengers at bay included those in Washington and Missouri. 

In the swing state of Michigan earlier this month, however, progressive Addul El-Sayed, who campaigned with Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders, eked out a victory against centrist candidate Haley Stevens despite over $60 million being spent on her behalf, largely from super PACs. 

El-Sayed, like other progressive candidates, campaigned on issues like medicare for all, getting money out of politics, taxing billionaire wealth and calling for an end to military aid for Israel. He has also been praised for his communication skills. 

In response to the U.S. President Donald Trump calling him "full of shit," El-Sayed shot back: "At least I don't let mine go all over the Oval Office." 

Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan's Democratic Senate primary in major victory for party's progressive wingMichigan's Democratic Senate primary puts spotlight on big money and pro-Israel lobby

El-Sayed's victory followed wins from progressive candidates who took on more moderate democrats in strongholds of New York and Colorado. 

Notably, in Maine, another battleground state, progressive Graham Platner delivered a win before he dropped out due to sexual assault allegations. 

Discontent among young voters 

Bhaskar Sunkara, president of left-leaning magazine The Nation and former vice chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, says El-Sayed's win and others like it are a "huge check" on the Democratic Party. 

"Voters, particularly young voters, are really discontent with the leadership of the party … and just generally feel that the Democratic Party doesn't stand for anything. It's not combative enough." 

Sunkara went on to say that El-Sayed is a better candidate than Hong with working-class voters. 

"I think there is a way in which some candidates have been tarred with stances they had in 2019, 2020. This sort of abolish the police, the discussion of whiteness or whatever else. Abdul never had that problem." 

Hong wasn't the only candidate backing off from past comments. 

New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made headlines earlier this week when asked about her past support for defunding the police. "I have a local city councilman that has this saying: 'Woke 1 was crazy,' " she said before laughing. 

Can progressives win key battleground states? 

While some in the progressive wing re-evaluate past positions that could alienate voters this election cycle, many moderate democrats continue to warn of liabilities in swing states. 

Fareed Zakaria, host of CNN's Sunday public affairs program GPS, cited Washington Post data to point out that while El-Sayed had the support of Michigan's most educated counties and college towns, his opponent did better in rural and lower-income areas. 

AnalysisWhat the Graham Platner scandal says about Democratic Party's troublesMore Americans than ever are identifying as political independents, poll shows

"The left has the passion, but the middle still has the votes needed to win in general elections," Zakaria said. 

Kate de Gruyter is the vice-president of communications at Third Way, a leading centrist democratic group that is spending $15 million between now and 2028 to discredit Democratic Socialism. 

"Their theory of the case is that they're somehow going to be able to persuade all these voters in the middle that they absolutely need to win in November to back their candidate. We've never seen that happen over the entirety of the Trump era," she said in an interview. 

De Gruyter added that El-Sayed's decision to campaign with controversial left-wing streamer Hasan Piker as one example of "a whole universe of things that Republican ad makers are salivating at."

De Gruyter went on to suggest that the reason Democrat Kamala Harris lost the presidential election in 2024 was that she was seen as too lax on issues like immigration and plagued by stances she'd taken in the past on "transgender policy." 

Democrats' autopsy of 2024 U.S. election blames Harris and 'identity politics' for lossKamala Harris says she 'might' make another presidential run in 2028

In the final weeks of the campaign. Trump's team ran an ad using a five-year old clip of Harris saying that "every transgender inmate in the prison system would have access" to taxpayer-funded gender transitions.

"The idea that we should move further left makes no sense at all," she said. 

The interesting thing is that while that can all be true, there are also plenty of arguments that suggest the opposite, according to Noel, the Georgetown associate professor. 

"And it can also be true that Harris actually lost because she was too tied to the establishment and Biden. And too close to Israel … progressives called her a cop. Either of those differences could have been enough because it was a fairly close race." 

Either way, Democrats are riding favourable waves into the midterms. 

Trump's polling is low. He has entered into an unpopular war in Iran. And all of this should help the Democrats, whether they're progressives or moderates in the mid-terms, said Noel, adding that if the Democrats don't do as well as expected there will be a lot of "what happened?"

"If all the progressive candidates lose and the centrist candidates win, well, that's going to be an easier story."

news.title: Taylor Swift Has Her Music Removed from Multiple TikTok Videos Posted By President Donald Trump’s Team
news.text:
Taylor Swift seemingly had her music removed from multiple TikTok videos posted by President Donald Trump’s social media team.
On Wednesday, August 12, the White House used Swift's 2021 track “I Bet You Think About Me” over footage of Trump, 80, speaking to supporters. A caption referenced the song’s lyrics, with the White House writing, “We know you think about us.”
However, as of late Wednesday, the TikTok video is now muted and features an onscreen caption announcing that “this sound isn’t available.”
This incident comes on the heels of the Team Trump TikTok account using Swift’s “August” in a campaign video on Saturday, August 8, along with the caption, “I’m sure Taylor Swift is going to be super excited we used her song.” Hours later, “August” was replaced by other music after an onscreen message explained that “the copyright owner hasn’t made this sound available in your country.”
Rolling Stone reported that Swift, 36, also recently quietly had her music removed from older TikTok videos posted by the president’s social media team.
Us has reached out to representatives for Swift and the White House for comment.
The White House routinely uses popular music in its social media videos without consulting the artists.
Katy Perry, Kesha and Ariana Grande have all condemned the White House this year for using their songs in social media content glorifying Trump’s divisive immigration policy and the war in Iran.
In October 2025, the White House admitted to intentionally antagonizing artists to generate more views for its social media content. At the time, there was outrage among Swift’s fans when the official White House TikTok account posted a video based on the singer-songwriter’s No. 1 hit “The Fate of Ophelia.”
“We made this video because we knew fake news media brands would breathlessly amplify them,” a White House spokesperson told Us at the time. “Congrats, you got played.”
More recently, Trump mocked Swift’s wedding to Kansas City Chiefs star Travis Kelce on July 4 before insisting during a July 6 press conference that he is more influential than Swift on TikTok.
“It was announced about two days ago. The new numbers just came out. You know who the No. 1 person in TikTok is by far? Trump, me. I’m No. 1,” Trump announced without citing his source. “Like, Taylor Swift was number 11. I’m No. 1 in TikTok by far.”
Swift has largely stayed away from directly engaging with Trump’s attacks though she did endorse his 2024 presidential opponent, former Vice President Kamala Harris.
“Recently I was made aware that AI of ‘me’ falsely endorsing Donald Trump’s presidential run was posted to his site,” she wrote at the time. “It really conjured up my fears around AI, and the dangers of spreading misinformation. It brought me to the conclusion that I need to be very transparent about my actual plans for this election as a voter. The simplest way to combat misinformation is with the truth.”
Swift went on, “I will be casting my vote for Kamala Harris and Tim Walz in the 2024 Presidential Election. I’m voting for @kamalaharris because she fights for the rights and causes I believe need a warrior to champion them. I think she is a steady-handed, gifted leader and I believe we can accomplish so much more in this country if we are led by calm and not chaos. I was so heartened and impressed by her selection of running mate @timwalz, who has been standing up for LGBTQ+ rights, IVF, and a woman’s right to her own body for decades.”
Trump ultimately defeated Harris, 61, in the November 2024 presidential election.

news.title: The Doomers Can’t Deny Trump’s Big Wins
news.text:
No, everything isn’t perfect, and we patriots should keep demanding more and more from the Trump 47 administration. Keep the pressure on. Keep the heat on. Don’t let anyone in Washington think that we’re just ready to settle. But on the other hand, don’t spaz out like a teenage girl whose parents just read her diary about what President Donald Trump has accomplished so far. Yeah, there have been disappointments. Here’s a flash: there are disappointments in life. You can’t always get what you want, but this administration tried really hard, and we might just get what we need.

Let’s review some of the typical complaints from Team All-Is-Lost. The war in Iran hasn’t yet been conclusively won. Millions upon millions of illegal aliens are still in the United States. We’re paying fat slobs to sit on their butts and gobble down Doritos that our welfare dollars pay for. Republicans are weak and soft, and haven’t passed the SAVE Act. Trust-fund communists are taking over the Democrat Party. The economy under Trump 47 hasn’t yet matched the economy under Trump 45. The budget is still out of control. Bureaucrats keep interfering in our agenda. Judges keep getting in the way of progress. Democrats keep getting in the way of progress. Progressives keep getting in the way of progress.

So, we should whine and cry, right? After all, what has Trump accomplished?

A lot. I don’t need a column for that. I need a book.

Let’s look at the border. It’s closed. The argument isn’t over how many thousands of Third World invaders we let in every day. The argument is now about the walls we are actually building — they’re really mad that we’re going to put up barriers in a national park instead of letting thousands of invaders trash it as they traipse through it. We have net-zero immigration right now. More foreigners are leaving than coming in. Think about that. Back in 2024, it was inconceivable that we would be where we are. Yet here we are. The biggest problem America faced has been solved, at least until America is stupid enough to elect a Democrat again. If Trump did nothing else during the last two years, this would be enough to make him a success.

And he’s done a hell of a lot more just on immigration. He unleashed ICE to toss hundreds of thousands of illegal aliens out, and the boot-out rate is increasing. We’re putting the temporary back in “Temporary Protected Status.” We’re banning immigration from many garbage countries and putting limits on H-1B visas. We’ve got the asylum adjudication machine up and moving — no more six years to your hearing date and no more soft-touch judges who grant asylum to anyone with a sob story. ICE is only going to get bigger. The invaders who will only leave the hard way are going to get their wish, and as the administration tightens the rules on giving free stuff to invaders who shouldn’t be here, more of them are going to pick up and leave. We’ve already seen the results. Foreigner job numbers have dropped, but American jobs have risen. Crime is down. Hell, even traffic is better in LA.

Let’s look at the federal government’s pinko feeding trough. We used to have USAID funding transgender mime troupes in Bolivia. We’ve defunded that crap, and a ton of leftist NGOs, as a result. Look at the map. Latin America is turning red because American money isn’t going to fund leftist parties. You could hear about it on NPR, but we’ve stopped giving them government money. Trump didn’t cut everything he wanted to cut, but he cut a lot. Who the hell did that before?

On the economy, yeah, gas prices have gone up because we’ve got to deal with the world as it is. But last month, inflation dropped — again. Take a look at your retirement accounts. They’ve gone up, up, up. Unless you’re a borderline mental defective, you understand that we’re not going to enter into a deflationary cycle. The way we’re going to have to deal with affordability is by growing wages, and that’s going to take time. Sorry, the good-economy wand is broken, but the good economy is still coming. Trump has cut taxes, including the kind that hit working people hardest. If Kamala Harris were here, we’d all be holding our gruel bowls begging “More, please.”

Sure, there’s a giant problem with healthcare. You know healthcare — it was called “Obamacare” until the people who created Obamacare realized how much Obamacare sucked. Do we have a solution yet? No, thanks to weak Republicans who refused to repeal it. But Trump’s doing something hugely important — preventing the single-payer socialized-medicine nightmare. The only people bummed about this are the people who think that medicine should be run by the same people who run the DMV.

How about Iran? I know, Trump promised no more forever wars. Well, Iran is about ending a forever war — one those 7th-century savages declared against us about 50 years ago. Oh no, they fought back. Pathetically, and tactically ineffectively, but yeah, they shot at us. They’ve actually killed a few of us. That’s why it’s called a “war.” But the United States has completely dominated the fight, and only idiots think that the Strait of Hormuz is somehow checkmated because a bunch of Iranians are saying so on X while millions of barrels of oil flow through every day. Yeah, finishing the job is hard, and it’s taking longer than our impatient society wants, but it will remove a huge strategic opponent from the board. Go short on the mullahs, if you’re smart — Trump’s going to finish this, and them.

Oh, and the Trump administration is still hunting down and eliminating scores of other terrorists. We have re-introduced something that has been missing on the part of our enemies for far too long — fear.

Let’s review some other wins. DEI is dead in the whole United States government. Trump’s defunding and banning gender mutilation. The U.S. military is back, not only putting up wins on the scoreboard, but posting record recruiting numbers after getting rid of the curse of DEI. We haven’t got the SAVE Act yet, but we’ve got Trump promulgating orders to curb some of the most blatant mail-in ballot abuses. We’re gutting regulations on everything from guns to mining to drilling and beyond.

Yeah, we’re getting resistance in the courts. Resistance doesn’t mean you’re losing. In this case, it means we’re winning. When some communist judge from the Eastern District of the Soviet Union decides that Trump’s not allowed to be president because of reasons and racism, and the DOJ appeals, the Trump administration wins about 95 percent of the time. Hell, the only time it lost, birthright citizenship, it still came out 5–4, which is closer than anyone with any glancing familiarity with the law ever imagined, and set the stage for new executive orders that will limit birth tourism.

We could go on and on. We could talk about the superstars that Trump’s brought aboard, from JD Vance to Marco Rubio, from Scott Bessent to Pete Hegseth. We could talk about tons of things that are driving the Left crazy, like beautifying Washington, D.C., and cutting crime. The persecuted patriots of J6 have been pardoned, as have the grandmas jailed for praying in abortion clinics. The FBI is no longer trying to frame the Commander-in-Chief and lock up moms who dared to raise their concerns at school board meetings.

We should be talking about these wins. Donald Trump should be talking about them, and when he holds his convention next month, I expect he will. That’s the real story: not the whining about the things we haven’t done yet, but about celebrating the things we have.

That’s why the blackpillers are so annoying. To be a doomer, you have to ignore the great things we have achieved. That’s ridiculous and unreasonable. Now, no one is saying that we can’t complain about mistakes and missteps. It’s saying that you have to understand that every human endeavor, especially something as complex and unwieldy as reversing course on the entire United States government, is going to have its share of mistakes and missteps. Adults understand that, and they don’t wet themselves every time some things don’t go their way.

Newsflash — some things are not going to go your way. Everything isn’t going to be fixed tomorrow. That doesn’t mean don’t complain — you should be complaining because that keeps the pressure on. Complain that we haven’t thrown out enough illegals, complain that we haven’t locked up enough criminals, complain that we haven’t killed enough Third World savages who threaten America. But don’t undermine the morale of our side by dwelling on what hasn’t been done yet to the exclusion of all the many things that Trump 47 has done so far.

Be dissatisfied with Donald Trump if you want. Think that he could be doing more. Again, keep the pressure on. Yeah, there are lots of problems and lots of things to do. Welcome to the world. Here’s another newsflash: everything is never going to get fixed. You’re not going to get to that shining city on the hill until they plant you six feet under.

But understand that life is about choices. We face a stark one. It is the Trump administration, with all its imperfections, versus a potential DSA communist regime that’s going to take your guns, take your liberty, and take your son’s genitals if he looks sideways at a Barbie doll. We had that choice in 2024, and we made the right one. We need to keep making it in 2026 and 2028. We have a long way to go, but dammit, don’t ever think we haven’t come a long way already.

news.title: Obama to Tell 'the Brothers' to Vote for El-Sayed
news.text:
Former President Barack Obama will likely campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, the far-left Democrat who just won Michigan's U.S. Senate primary.

The two spoke after the primary, and El-Sayed publicly said he hopes Obama will campaign for him. Michigan could determine control of the Senate, and Obama remains the most popular Democrat.

El-Sayed won despite performing poorly among black primary voters. His coalition skewed younger, whiter, college-educated and progressive. In Detroit, Michigan's largest majority-black city, El-Sayed's opponent won more than 60 percent of the Democrat Senate vote. That may work in a Democrat primary. But will it work in November?

Enter Obama.

During the 2024 presidential campaign, Obama visited a Kamala Harris campaign office in Pittsburgh and said he wanted to "speak some truths." He complained that enthusiasm for Harris was weaker than when he ran and said the problem "seems to be more pronounced with the brothers."

Obama said: "You're coming up with all kinds of reasons and excuses. I've got a problem with that," he said, suggesting some Black men "just aren't feeling the idea of having a woman as president."

Apparently, some of "the brothers" remained unpersuaded. Pew Research Center's validated-voter analysis later estimated that 21 percent of black men voted for Donald Trump. Nevertheless, Obama will probably go to Michigan and explain to black voters who rejected El-Sayed in the primary why they should vote for him in November. After all, Obama and El-Sayed are closely aligned on policy.

Take healthcare. El-Sayed supports Medicare for All. Obama repeatedly said the ideal healthcare plan would be single-payer. "If I were starting a system from scratch," Obama said in 2009, "then I think that the idea of moving towards a single-payer system could very well make sense." Near the end of his second term, Obama said, "If I was starting from scratch, I probably would have supported a single-payer system."

Then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid called it a goal. Asked in 2013 whether Obamacare was ultimately a step toward single-payer healthcare, Reid answered, "Yes, yes. Absolutely, yes."

Like Obama, El-Sayed chastises "the rich" for "not paying their fair share in taxes." Like Obama, who said racism is part of America's "DNA," El-Sayed believes racism remains a serious problem.

How far from Obama are these "far-left" Democrats? Last year, Obama called Democratic Socialist Zohran Mamdani during his campaign for New York City mayor, praised his campaign and reportedly offered to serve as a "sounding board."

On Israel, there isn't much daylight between the two. El-Sayed has called the Israeli government "evil," "bloodthirsty" and a "rogue state." He declined to directly answer when asked, "Do you believe Israel has a right to exist?" Obama never went that far. He repeatedly defended Israel's legitimacy and security.

But Obama and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu repeatedly clashed. Netanyahu fiercely opposed Obama's Iran nuclear deal, warning that Tehran could not be trusted. Israel obtained an archive of Iranian nuclear documents that Netanyahu said proved Iran was lying about its nuclear-weapons activities and was not abiding by the terms of the deal. The Obama-Netanyahu relationship became so poisonous that a senior Obama administration official reportedly called Netanyahu "chickens***." The White House distanced itself from the insult, but the hostility between the two leaders was no secret.

What explains El-Sayed's weakness among black primary voters? In 2020, he explicitly said, "I believe we need to defund the police." Polls show blacks want the level of policing in their community to remain the same, if not increased. Blacks are disproportionately victims of crime. Tupac Shakur said: "The same crime element that white people are scared of black people are scared of ... Just because we black, we get along with the killers? What is that? We need protection, too."

El-Sayed wants to abolish ICE, despite studies showing a connection between unskilled illegal aliens and lower wages and greater unemployment among black workers in the same skill group.

This brings us back to Obama. El-Sayed needs black voters who did not particularly want him. Democrats need Michigan to gain control of the Senate.

So, expect the former president to show up. And when he does, Obama will give "the brothers" a message. You may not have wanted this candidate. His positions may be against your self-interests.

But vote for him anyway.

news.title: New 2028 presidential frontrunner has emerged on a key prediction market site
news.text:
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is now the frontrunner to become the 2028 Democratic presidential nominee, according to Polymarket odds, marking the first time she has led the pack. 

As of Wednesday evening, 21 percent of traders backed the New York progressive, who was trailed by California Governor Gavin Newsom at 17 percent. On rival prediction site Kalshi, the results were the same, with Ocasio-Cortez narrowly topping Newsom. 

Meanwhile, conventional political polls still put former Vice President Kamala Harris at the top spot, with Newsom in second and AOC in a distant fourth. 

Ocasio-Cortez has not announced a formal presidential bid, nor has she sworn one off. Right now she’s focused on helping Democrats win the midterms, she recently told The Independent.

“I think my main focus is really genuinely just the midterms right now, and we have to make sure that we win this majority,” she said.

Ocasio-Cortez recently made headlines for detailing the process of freezing her eggs on social media and reflecting on the precarious state of women’s healthcare in America.

“In the political context that we're in, in an administration that is dedicated to politicizing women’s bodies and taking our choices away from us and punishing us around decisions to be pregnant or not be pregnant — and, frankly, this administration has made pregnancy more dangerous than probably at any point in the last 30 plus years — we’re gonna take our power back,” she told her followers. 

She also generated considerable discussion in political circles for branding 2020-era “woke” ideas “crazy,” reflecting that while many of the social justice-focused discussions of that era were “fruitful,” the "rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today.” 

An AOC 2028 bid would be the latest test of whether Democrats will move further to the left, in line with rising Democratic socialists and progressives such as New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, or whether the party will tack back to the center.

In many ways, the party is still reeling from the 2024 election, where Harris replaced President Joe Biden in the late stages of the race and lost to Donald Trump, despite the Republican campaigning under a cloud of lawsuits and government investigations. 

Considerable divides remain in the party over issues including healthcare, U.S. support for Israel and immigration. 

The Democrats are projected to retake at least the House in the midterms, according to polling, on the back of high gas prices and an unpopular war in Iran.
news.summary: Democrats still reeling from the 2024 election, where Harris replaced President Joe Biden in the late stages of the race and lost to Donald Trump

news.title: Trump sued over sale of access to Truth Social posts
news.text:
WASHINGTON - Two US media groups on Wednesday sued President Donald Trump over his move to charge for early access to his often market-moving Truth Social posts.

The lawsuit, filed in New York by The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation, states that the scheme is "extraordinary, corrupt and unconstitutional."

Subscribers to the paid service are supposed to get almost instantaneous access to Trump's messages on the Truth Social platform -- crucial seconds ahead of the general public.

The billionaire Republican often uses the platform to announce huge news, ranging from developments in the Iran war to trade tariffs, all of which can instantly send market values tumbling or soaring.

Early access to the service can cost up to $100,000 per month, or $60,000 per month if users commit to three years, according to Wednesday's lawsuit.

"This scheme is profoundly corrupt. The President stands to gain financially by giving 'market-moving' government information to those who are willing and able to pay his personal company," a court filing says.

Trump Media & Technology Group, the company running the platform, has dismissed concerns over the product, which is called Truth API and was first unveiled in mid-July. 

- Calls for probe -

The Intercept, a nonprofit US news outlet, and Freedom of the Press Foundation, which operates a database tracking Truth Social posts, argue that the paid service hinders their ability to properly cover Trump.

"Timely access to the President's posts is critical for both groups," the filing states, asking the court to declare Truth API as unlawful and block future posts.

Several Democratic lawmakers have called for a probe into the service by the Securities and Exchange Commission, which regulates US markets.

Trump Media interim CEO Kevin McGurn said this week that Truth API is already generating revenue with 10 customer agreements signed, though he did not identify the clients.

The Wall Street Journal has reported that trading companies were among the first to subscribe to the service.

On Monday, Trump Media posted a ten-fold jump in losses for the second quarter of 2026, linked to declines in values of its digital assets.

Trump, like his close relatives, is alleged to have made billions of dollars in his second White House term through cryptocurrency ventures, property deals, stock trades and payouts from lawsuits.

Forbes, a financial media outlet, has estimated that Trump's net worth shot up from $2.3 billion to $6.5 billion since 2024, when he won the election over Kamala Harris.

news.title: STATESIDE: Will Upper Midwest finally upend Trump-effect?
news.text:
YESTERDAY morning brought to American TV screens and on-line news feeds some news that surprised many observers. It may presage results in the upcoming November elections that seem poised to bring an end to what has amounted to one-party rule in Washington since president Donald Trump was reelected nearly two years ago.

Taken together with some results from last week, Americans are beginning to see the outlines of what is to come politically at just about the time most of them are starting to stir around and actually pay attention to politics and how it may affect their economic, social, and political future.

In Michigan, Minnesota, and Wisconsin, primary elections for both Democrats and Republicans were held. These Upper Midwest states, all once part of a redoubtable ‘blue wall’ of reasonably reliably Democratic states, have shown themselves to be susceptible to Trump and the Republican message in more recent elections such as the one that returned Trump to the White House and accorded to him slender, but often effective, majorities in both American legislative houses of Congress.

Michigan voted last week. The big story here was the victory in the Democratic Senate primary of Dr. Abdul El-Sayed. El-Sayed, 41, who was born in a Detroit suburb but whose political prospects would doubtless be strengthened considerably if his name were Tom Smith, graduated from the University of Michigan with Highest Distinction in 2007 and delivered that year's commencement address. 

Former US President Bill Clinton, whose commencement speech followed El-Sayed's, told the huge audience that "I don't want to embarrass your senior speaker, but I wish every person in the world who believes that we are fated to have a clash of civilizations, and cannot reach across the religious divides, could have heard you speak today." According to El-Sayed, Clinton approached him after the ceremony and encouraged him to consider public service.

This scene must have been reminiscent for Clinton of his own undergraduate encounter with then-US president John F Kennedy, nearly 50 years previously.

El-Sayed went on to earn graduate degrees from Columbia and Oxford Universities and served for several years as the medical director of Wayne County, Michigan, where Detroit is located. An ambitious political operator who is good in front of crowds, El-Sayed in victory last week dealt a major blow to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), whose political action committee spent more than $30 million to attack him. 

According to American census data, the US city with the largest percentage of Arab Americans is Dearborn, Michigan, a southwestern suburb of Detroit, at nearly 40%. The Detroit metropolitan area is home to the largest concentration of Arab Americans in the country.

El-Sayed supports regulated capitalism, Medicare for all, enforcing an arms embargo on Israel, and abolishing ICE. He ran for governor in 2018, placing second to popular incumbent Gretchen Whitmer in the Democratic primary. He has called the humanitarian crisis still ravaging Gaza “a genocide” and is critical of US aid to Israel.

After El-Sayed’s primary victory in an unusually bitter, fractious campaign over a candidate actively supported by the Democratic party leadership in Washington, the Michigan Dems seem to have come together fairly quickly in seeking unity to retain a key Senate seat in November.

Minnesota and Wisconsin voted on Tuesday. In the Minnesota, there is continuing fallout over three developments during the past couple of years. First, governor Tim Walz was surprisingly picked by Kamala Harris as her 2024 running mate, reportedly in large measure because he was unlikely to upstage or rival her as alternative choices such as dynamic Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro might have done. 

Walz started strongly as a national campaigner, but began to fizzle down the stretch and is not generally regarded as having been of much benefit to Harris’s ultimately losing campaign against Trump. After their Democratic defeat two years ago, Walz quietly left the national stage and thoughts of his running for re-election as governor soon evaporated.

Walz is at the centre of the second development as well. On his watch as governor, the Democratic-dominated Minnesota state administration has faced intense criticism over its handling of fraud in several significant state-managed programs that federal prosecutors say could end up costing the taxpayers over $9 billion. This scandal broke at the beginning of last year and was largely overshadowed by the ICE invasion of Minneapolis, but it’s one of the most dramatic bits of evidence ever to support long-standing Republican charges of mismanagement and corruption in massive Democratic-supported social welfare programs all across the US.

The third, decisive, factor in Minnesota is ICE. We all are well aware of the Trump administration’s decision to make an example of traditionally left-leaning Minneapolis by deploying ICE agents in great numbers to the city and environs, essentially to make an example of the area. 

Operation MetroSurge was an operation launched last December by United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) with the stated purpose of apprehending undocumented immigrants and deporting them. Operation Metro Surge initially targeted the Twin Cities (Minneapolis and Saint Paul), and later expanded to all of Minnesota. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) called it "the largest immigration enforcement operation ever carried out.”

This operation was characterized by an escalation in the severity of ICE tactics, harassment, and threats against observers. It resulted in the killing of two US citizens and the arrest of more than 3,000 people. To describe Operation Metro Surge as a calamitous failure hardly does justice to how fundamentally stupid and misguided it was. 

But it did let the careless Dems off the hook for their stupendous program mismanagement and faith in the feckless Tim Walz, and Tuesday’s results seem to have ensured that the governorship and US Senate seat now in Democratic hands will remain blue after November.

In Wisconsin, the results in the Democratic primary election to pick a candidate for governor were startling. The contest had been tumultuous almost from the start, with contenders entering and even leaving the race during its twisting course. Meanwhile, the Republicans chose a sitting congressman, Tom Tiffany, who will carry Trump’s endorsement into a general election campaign he is almost certain to lose. Tiffany, boasting a 100 percent record of supporting everything Trump has demanded of his subservient Republican-dominated Congress, still clings to 2020 election denying as a badge of honour and as a mark of obeisance to Trump’s hegemony in the GOP. 

For the longest time, it looked like Tiffany would nonetheless prevail in November, as his Democratic opponent looked sure to be a state assemblywoman, Francesca Hong. Hong, born in Wisconsin to Korean immigrant parents and the first Asian American to serve in the Wisconsin state assembly, is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America and quickly became a campaign tag line.

In a Nov 16, 2020, social media post Hong has since deleted, she said the US should get rid of Thanksgiving as an annual holiday. The event is “celebrating colonialism,” she wrote at the time, and by inference Thanksgiving excuses the diseases spread by European settlers that “killed [indigenous] people."

Even the most inept and inexperienced Republican operative would have relished the opportunity to write campaign ads impugning an opponent who advocated for abolishing America’s great autumnal feast holiday. But alas for the Republicans, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, a bespectacled black candidate, surged back into the race and won by just a relative handful of votes to re-calibrate the upcoming race for governor. 

Crowley dropped out of the governor’s race on July 8, saying he didn’t see a path to victory with Hong leading by as many as 20 percentage points in the polls. He rejoined it on July 18, less than a month before Tuesday’s primary, after strong encouragement from national and state Democratic leaders who foresaw the unimaginable in a Tiffany win despite Trump’s serious unpopularity.

With the backing of the Democratic incumbent governor Tony Evers, Crowley pulled out the narrow win on the argument that he was the better match-up against Tiffany. There can be no doubt that assertion is true.

There’s much speculation that if progressive and moderate Democrats can just get along, they’ll rout Trump and the GOP in November. The Upper Midwest just offered a possible template for success.

news.title: Jen Psaki Said It Out Loud: Party Leaders ‘Really Selected’ Nominees
news.text:
Jen Psaki may have just said one of the most revealing things I've heard from a former Democratic White House official in years.

The former Biden White House press secretary, who now hosts The Briefing with Jen Psaki on MS Now, was discussing Democrat primaries when she casually acknowledged how the system once worked:

"Party leadership really selected the nominees."

Jen Psaki admits on MSNBC that Democratic Party leadership used to “SELECT” the nominees, and nobody was allowed to say it out loud until now.PSAKI: “We both remember well when party leadership really selected the nominees.”“Now, you would never say it that way exactly, but… pic.twitter.com/puZEN4FVvX— The Vigilant Fox 🦊 (@VigilantFox) August 12, 2026

Psaki added that nobody would have described it quite so openly at the time.

Listen to and read her words again: Party leadership really selected the nominees.

Americans should hear that sentence everywhere because it comes from somebody who spent years inside Democratic politics, including senior communications jobs in the Obama and Biden administrations.

Psaki wasn't some outsider guessing about smoke-filled rooms; she worked in the rooms.

Bernie Sanders supporters learned a painful version of the lesson in 2016. Leaked internal emails exposed hostility toward Sanders inside the Democratic National Committee during his primary battle with Hillary Clinton.

The DNC eventually issued what it called a "deep and sincere apology" to Sanders and his supporters for the conduct revealed in those messages.

“On behalf of everyone at the DNC, we want to offer a deep and sincere apology to Senator Sanders, his supporters, and the entire Democratic Party for the inexcusable remarks made over email. These comments do not reflect the values of the DNC or our steadfast commitment to neutrality during the nominating process. The DNC does not — and will not — tolerate disrespectful language exhibited toward our candidates. Individual staffers have also rightfully apologized for their comments, and the DNC is taking appropriate action to ensure it never happens again.“We are embarking on a convention today that — thanks to the great efforts of Secretary Clinton, her team, Senator Sanders, his team, and the entire Democratic Party — will show a forward-thinking and optimistic vision for America, as compared to the dark and pessimistic vision that the GOP presented last week in Cleveland. Our focus is on electing Hillary Clinton, Tim Kaine and Democrats across the country, thanks to Democratic Party that is strong, unified, and poised for victory in November.”

Clinton still won more primary votes and pledged delegates, so I won't claim somebody secretly changed ballots to steal the nomination from Sanders. The documented problem was party neutrality.

Democrat officials themselves apologized after internal communications showed the supposedly neutral organization wasn't behaving very neutrally.

Then came 2024.

Joe Biden won the Democratic presidential primaries and dropped out in July. Democrat voters never received another presidential primary in which they could choose his replacement.

Kamala Harris became the only candidate who qualified for the DNC's virtual roll-call ballot after 3,923 delegates signed petitions supporting her.

A few days later, 4,567 delegates voted for Harris, giving her 99% support among participating delegates. She became the Democratic presidential nominee without ever winning a presidential primary for the job in 2024.

The next steps in the nominating process include the certification of the roll call by the Convention Secretary Jason Rae, and the acceptance of the nomination by Vice President Harris and her running mate, certified by DNCC Chair Minyon Moore. Delegates will then celebrate the nomination through a celebratory Roll Call at the in-person Convention, gaveled in by DNC Chair Jaime Harrison and DNCC Chair Minyon Moore.Statement from DNC Chair Jaime Harrison and DNCC Chair Minyon Moore:“With the support of 99% of all participating delegates in the virtual roll call, Vice President Harris has historic momentum at her back as we embark on the final steps in officially certifying her as our Party’s nominee. We thank the thousands of delegates from all across the country who took seriously their responsibility throughout this process to make their voices – and the voices of their communities – heard. As we prepare to certify the nomination alongside Convention Secretary Rae, we know that we are all a part of an important piece of history. Soon, it will be time to come together in Chicago, where we will celebrate together and make clear to the American people that the Democratic Party is the party of freedom, of democracy, of rights, and of the people.” 

Now Psaki says party leaders once "really selected the nominees."

Maybe Democrats will argue she was merely describing an older political era when endorsements, donors, and party bosses carried greater influence.

Her explanation still deserves attention because 2016 and 2024 make the subject anything but ancient history.

Democrats spent years presenting themselves as guardians of democracy while warning Americans that Republicans threatened voters' voices. Meanwhile, their own recent history contains a national party apologizing for misconduct toward one presidential candidate and later nominating another candidate whom Democrat primary voters never selected for president.

Psaki's sentence belongs outside the cable-news echo chamber.

Put it on television; put it online; yell it from the rooftops!

Democrat voters especially deserve to hear it because sometimes the most revealing political confession isn't dragged out under the oath.

Sometimes somebody vapid just says it out loud.
